# Science · Ages 4–5 · Food and digestion

Q: Where do you put food when you eat?
A) Mouth*  B) Ear  C) Nose  D) Elbow
Why: Food enters through the mouth.

Q: What helps you bite an apple?
A) Lips  B) Teeth*  C) Ears  D) Eyelashes
Why: Teeth break food into smaller pieces.

Q: What do you do to food with your teeth?
A) Hear it  B) Blink it  C) Chew it*  D) Breathe it
Why: Chewing breaks food into smaller pieces.

Q: What helps move food around your mouth?
A) Eyebrow  B) Knee  C) Ear  D) Tongue*
Why: The tongue moves food around the mouth.

Q: What is the wet liquid in your mouth called?
A) Saliva*  B) Blood  C) Bile  D) Urine
Why: Saliva wets food and helps you swallow.
Source: [https://www.niddk.nih.gov/health-information/digestive-diseases/digestive-system-how-it-works](https://www.niddk.nih.gov/health-information/digestive-diseases/digestive-system-how-it-works)

Q: What do you do after chewing your food?
A) Blink  B) Swallow*  C) Listen  D) Clap
Why: Swallowing moves food from the mouth towards the stomach.

Q: Which body part mixes food in your tummy?
A) Heart  B) Lung  C) Stomach*  D) Brain
Why: Stomach muscles mix food with digestive juices.

Q: Where is your stomach?
A) On your head  B) Outside your knee  C) Inside your shoe  D) Inside your body*
Why: The stomach is an internal organ.

Q: What does food give us for playing?
A) Energy*  B) Wings  C) Sunlight  D) Feathers
Why: Food provides energy for body activities.

Q: What does food help children do?
A) Turn into stone  B) Grow*  C) Make sunlight  D) Become invisible
Why: Nutrients support growth and body repair.

Q: Which is a drink your body needs?
A) Paint  B) Petrol  C) Water*  D) Glue
Why: The body needs water for its normal functions.

Q: What goes into your mouth when you take a bite?
A) Light  B) Sound  C) Smoke  D) Food*
Why: Eating brings food into the digestive system.

Q: Which teeth are at the front of your mouth?
A) Front teeth*  B) Back teeth  C) Kneecaps  D) Ribs
Why: Front teeth have edges suited to cutting food.

Q: Which teeth help crush food at the back?
A) Eyelashes  B) Back teeth*  C) Front teeth only  D) Fingernails
Why: Back teeth crush and grind food.

Q: Where does food go after the stomach?
A) Ear  B) Heart  C) Small intestine*  D) Lung
Why: The stomach empties into the small intestine.
Source: [https://www.niddk.nih.gov/health-information/digestive-diseases/digestive-system-how-it-works](https://www.niddk.nih.gov/health-information/digestive-diseases/digestive-system-how-it-works)

Q: What do we call the parts of food the body can use?
A) Pebbles  B) Bubbles  C) Shadows  D) Nutrients*
Why: Nutrients support energy, growth and repair.

Q: What carries useful parts of food around the body?
A) Blood*  B) Hair  C) Air in the ears  D) Tooth enamel
Why: Blood carries many nutrients to body tissues.

Q: Which organ helps break food down?
A) Eye  B) Stomach*  C) Ear  D) Kneecap
Why: The stomach helps digest food.

Q: What does your body do with food it cannot use?
A) Stores it in hair  B) Turns it into teeth  C) Passes it out as poo*  D) Breathes it all out
Why: Undigested material leaves the body as faeces.

Q: Which goes in the right order?
A) Stomach → mouth  B) Ear → knee  C) Lung → ear  D) Mouth → stomach*
Why: Food moves from the mouth towards the stomach.

# Science · Ages 6–8 · Food and digestion

Q: Where does food enter your digestive system?
A) Ear  B) Mouth*  C) Nose  D) Elbow
Why: Food enters through the mouth.

Q: Which hard mouth parts cut and crush food?
A) Lips  B) Ears  C) Teeth*  D) Eyelashes
Why: Teeth break food into smaller pieces.

Q: What is the name for breaking food up with your teeth?
A) Hear it  B) Blink it  C) Breathe it  D) Chew it*
Why: Chewing breaks food into smaller pieces.

Q: Which muscular part moves food while you chew?
A) Tongue*  B) Eyebrow  C) Knee  D) Ear
Why: The tongue moves food around the mouth.

Q: What liquid moistens food before you swallow?
A) Blood  B) Saliva*  C) Bile  D) Urine
Why: Saliva wets food and helps you swallow.

Q: What action sends chewed food towards your stomach?
A) Blink  B) Listen  C) Swallow*  D) Clap
Why: Swallowing moves food from the mouth towards the stomach.

Q: Which organ churns food after you swallow?
A) Heart  B) Lung  C) Brain  D) Stomach*
Why: Stomach muscles mix food with digestive juices.

Q: Which description of the stomach is correct?
A) Inside your body*  B) On your head  C) Outside your knee  D) Inside your shoe
Why: The stomach is an internal organ.

Q: What does food supply for running and playing?
A) Wings  B) Energy*  C) Sunlight  D) Feathers
Why: Food provides energy for body activities.

Q: Besides supplying energy, what does food help your body do?
A) Turn into stone  B) Make sunlight  C) Grow*  D) Become invisible
Why: Nutrients support growth and body repair.

Q: Which liquid is essential for the body to work?
A) Paint  B) Petrol  C) Glue  D) Water*
Why: The body needs water for its normal functions.

Q: Which belongs in the digestive system when you eat?
A) Food*  B) Light  C) Sound  D) Smoke
Why: Eating brings food into the digestive system.

Q: Which teeth help cut into a piece of food?
A) Back teeth  B) Front teeth*  C) Kneecaps  D) Ribs
Why: Front teeth have edges suited to cutting food.

Q: Which teeth have broad surfaces for grinding food?
A) Eyelashes  B) Front teeth only  C) Back teeth*  D) Fingernails
Why: Back teeth crush and grind food.

Q: Which organ receives food after it leaves the stomach?
A) Ear  B) Heart  C) Lung  D) Small intestine*
Why: The stomach empties into the small intestine.
Source: [https://www.niddk.nih.gov/health-information/digestive-diseases/digestive-system-how-it-works](https://www.niddk.nih.gov/health-information/digestive-diseases/digestive-system-how-it-works)

Q: What are useful substances in food called?
A) Nutrients*  B) Pebbles  C) Bubbles  D) Shadows
Why: Nutrients support energy, growth and repair.

Q: What carries many absorbed nutrients to body cells?
A) Hair  B) Blood*  C) Air in the ears  D) Tooth enamel
Why: Blood carries many nutrients to body tissues.

Q: Which belongs to the digestive system?
A) Eye  B) Ear  C) Stomach*  D) Kneecap
Why: The stomach helps digest food.

Q: What happens to undigested waste after food passes through the gut?
A) Stores it in hair  B) Turns it into teeth  C) Breathes it all out  D) Passes it out as poo*
Why: Undigested material leaves the body as faeces.

Q: Which shows part of the journey of food?
A) Mouth → stomach*  B) Stomach → mouth  C) Ear → knee  D) Lung → ear
Why: Food moves from the mouth towards the stomach.

# Science · Ages 9–11 · Food and digestion

Q: What is another name for the oesophagus?
A) Gullet*  B) Windpipe  C) Aorta  D) Colon
Why: The oesophagus carries swallowed food to the stomach.

Q: What moves food along the gut in waves?
A) Diffusion  B) Peristalsis*  C) Filtration  D) Evaporation
Why: Peristalsis pushes food through the digestive tract.
Source: [https://training.seer.cancer.gov/anatomy/digestive/?view=searchengine](https://training.seer.cancer.gov/anatomy/digestive/?view=searchengine)

Q: Where does starch digestion begin?
A) Large intestine  B) Rectum  C) Mouth*  D) Gall bladder
Why: Saliva contains an enzyme that starts starch digestion.

Q: What do digestive enzymes do?
A) Pump blood  B) Build tooth enamel directly  C) Carry sound  D) Break large food molecules into smaller ones*
Why: Enzymes speed up chemical breakdown.
Source: [https://training.seer.cancer.gov/anatomy/digestive/?view=searchengine](https://training.seer.cancer.gov/anatomy/digestive/?view=searchengine)

Q: What is chyme?
A) Partly digested food mixed with stomach juices*  B) Stored bile  C) A type of bone  D) A red blood cell
Why: Stomach mixing produces a semi-liquid mixture called chyme.

Q: Which organ makes bile?
A) Gall bladder  B) Liver*  C) Kidney  D) Spleen
Why: The liver produces bile.
Source: [https://www.niddk.nih.gov/health-information/digestive-diseases/digestive-system-how-it-works](https://www.niddk.nih.gov/health-information/digestive-diseases/digestive-system-how-it-works)

Q: Where is bile stored between meals?
A) Pancreas  B) Stomach  C) Gall bladder*  D) Rectum
Why: The gall bladder stores bile before release.

Q: What does bile help digest?
A) Water  B) Oxygen  C) Minerals only  D) Fats*
Why: Bile disperses fats into small droplets.

Q: Which organ makes pancreatic juice?
A) Pancreas*  B) Lung  C) Heart  D) Urinary bladder
Why: The pancreas delivers digestive juice to the small intestine.
Source: [https://www.niddk.nih.gov/health-information/digestive-diseases/digestive-system-how-it-works](https://www.niddk.nih.gov/health-information/digestive-diseases/digestive-system-how-it-works)

Q: Where are most digested nutrients absorbed?
A) Oesophagus  B) Small intestine*  C) Rectum  D) Mouth
Why: Most nutrient absorption occurs in the small intestine.
Source: [https://www.niddk.nih.gov/health-information/digestive-diseases/digestive-system-how-it-works](https://www.niddk.nih.gov/health-information/digestive-diseases/digestive-system-how-it-works)

Q: What are villi?
A) Teeth in the stomach  B) Air sacs  C) Tiny projections that help absorption*  D) Heart valves
Why: Villi increase the surface available for absorption.

Q: What does the large intestine absorb?
A) Light  B) Sound  C) Nitrogen gas only  D) Water*
Why: Water recovery helps form faeces.

Q: Where are faeces stored before release?
A) Rectum*  B) Duodenum  C) Stomach  D) Liver
Why: The rectum holds faeces before release.

Q: What protects the stomach lining from its contents?
A) Haemoglobin  B) Mucus*  C) Earwax  D) Insulin
Why: Mucus helps shield the lining from gastric contents.

Q: What is the first part of the small intestine?
A) Ileum  B) Rectum  C) Duodenum*  D) Colon
Why: The duodenum is the first small-intestinal section.

Q: What is the middle part of the small intestine?
A) Caecum  B) Rectum  C) Oesophagus  D) Jejunum*
Why: The jejunum follows the duodenum.

Q: What is the last part of the small intestine?
A) Ileum*  B) Stomach  C) Jejunum  D) Oesophagus
Why: The ileum is the final small-intestinal section.

Q: What are proteins broken down into?
A) Red blood cells  B) Amino acids*  C) Bone crystals  D) Vitamins
Why: Proteins are built from amino acids.

Q: Which is mechanical digestion?
A) An enzyme splitting starch  B) Nutrients entering blood  C) Teeth grinding food*  D) Bile production
Why: Grinding physically breaks food into smaller pieces.

Q: What is absorption?
A) Only chewing  B) Only swallowing  C) Production of bile  D) Movement of nutrients across the gut lining*
Why: Absorption transfers digested nutrients into the body.
Source: [https://training.seer.cancer.gov/anatomy/digestive/?view=searchengine](https://training.seer.cancer.gov/anatomy/digestive/?view=searchengine)

# Science · Ages 12–14 · Food and digestion

Q: Which term refers to the food-carrying gullet?
A) Windpipe  B) Gullet*  C) Aorta  D) Colon
Why: The oesophagus carries swallowed food to the stomach.

Q: What is the name for coordinated contractions that propel food?
A) Diffusion  B) Filtration  C) Peristalsis*  D) Evaporation
Why: Peristalsis pushes food through the digestive tract.
Source: [https://training.seer.cancer.gov/anatomy/digestive/?view=searchengine](https://training.seer.cancer.gov/anatomy/digestive/?view=searchengine)

Q: Which location begins the chemical breakdown of starch?
A) Large intestine  B) Rectum  C) Gall bladder  D) Mouth*
Why: Saliva contains an enzyme that starts starch digestion.
Source: [https://www.niddk.nih.gov/health-information/digestive-diseases/digestive-system-how-it-works](https://www.niddk.nih.gov/health-information/digestive-diseases/digestive-system-how-it-works)

Q: What is the main role of enzymes in chemical digestion?
A) Break large food molecules into smaller ones*  B) Pump blood  C) Build tooth enamel directly  D) Carry sound
Why: Enzymes speed up chemical breakdown.
Source: [https://training.seer.cancer.gov/anatomy/digestive/?view=searchengine](https://training.seer.cancer.gov/anatomy/digestive/?view=searchengine)

Q: What name describes the mixture leaving the stomach?
A) Stored bile  B) Partly digested food mixed with stomach juices*  C) A type of bone  D) A red blood cell
Why: Stomach mixing produces a semi-liquid mixture called chyme.

Q: Where is bile produced before storage or use?
A) Gall bladder  B) Kidney  C) Liver*  D) Spleen
Why: The liver produces bile.
Source: [https://www.niddk.nih.gov/health-information/digestive-diseases/digestive-system-how-it-works](https://www.niddk.nih.gov/health-information/digestive-diseases/digestive-system-how-it-works)

Q: Which organ stores and concentrates bile?
A) Pancreas  B) Stomach  C) Rectum  D) Gall bladder*
Why: The gall bladder stores bile before release.
Source: [https://www.niddk.nih.gov/health-information/digestive-diseases/digestive-system-how-it-works](https://www.niddk.nih.gov/health-information/digestive-diseases/digestive-system-how-it-works)

Q: Bile is particularly important in processing which nutrient group?
A) Fats*  B) Water  C) Oxygen  D) Minerals only
Why: Bile disperses fats into small droplets.

Q: Which organ supplies digestive enzymes through a pancreatic duct?
A) Lung  B) Pancreas*  C) Heart  D) Urinary bladder
Why: The pancreas delivers digestive juice to the small intestine.

Q: Which gut region absorbs most nutrients from food?
A) Oesophagus  B) Rectum  C) Small intestine*  D) Mouth
Why: Most nutrient absorption occurs in the small intestine.
Source: [https://www.niddk.nih.gov/health-information/digestive-diseases/digestive-system-how-it-works](https://www.niddk.nih.gov/health-information/digestive-diseases/digestive-system-how-it-works)

Q: What are the finger-like projections of the small-intestinal lining?
A) Teeth in the stomach  B) Air sacs  C) Heart valves  D) Tiny projections that help absorption*
Why: Villi increase the surface available for absorption.

Q: Which substance is recovered from gut contents in the colon?
A) Water*  B) Light  C) Sound  D) Nitrogen gas only
Why: Water recovery helps form faeces.

Q: Which final gut region stores faeces before defaecation?
A) Duodenum  B) Rectum*  C) Stomach  D) Liver
Why: The rectum holds faeces before release.

Q: Which secretion helps protect the gastric lining?
A) Haemoglobin  B) Earwax  C) Mucus*  D) Insulin
Why: Mucus helps shield the lining from gastric contents.

Q: Which section receives chyme directly from the stomach?
A) Ileum  B) Rectum  C) Colon  D) Duodenum*
Why: The duodenum is the first small-intestinal section.

Q: Which small-intestinal section lies between duodenum and ileum?
A) Jejunum*  B) Caecum  C) Rectum  D) Oesophagus
Why: The jejunum follows the duodenum.

Q: Which small-intestinal section leads towards the large intestine?
A) Stomach  B) Ileum*  C) Jejunum  D) Oesophagus
Why: The ileum is the final small-intestinal section.

Q: Which smaller molecules result from complete protein digestion?
A) Red blood cells  B) Bone crystals  C) Amino acids*  D) Vitamins
Why: Proteins are built from amino acids.

Q: Which process changes food size without breaking chemical bonds?
A) An enzyme splitting starch  B) Nutrients entering blood  C) Bile production  D) Teeth grinding food*
Why: Grinding physically breaks food into smaller pieces.

Q: Which description distinguishes absorption from digestion?
A) Movement of nutrients across the gut lining*  B) Only chewing  C) Only swallowing  D) Production of bile
Why: Absorption transfers digested nutrients into the body.
Source: [https://training.seer.cancer.gov/anatomy/digestive/?view=searchengine](https://training.seer.cancer.gov/anatomy/digestive/?view=searchengine)

# Science · Ages 15–16 · Food and digestion

Q: Why does emulsifying fat help digestion?
A) Greater surface area for lipase*  B) Fat becomes protein  C) Enzymes become unnecessary  D) Absorption stops
Why: Smaller droplets expose more surface to enzyme action.

Q: Which enzyme digests fats?
A) Amylase  B) Lipase*  C) Pepsin  D) Haemoglobin
Why: Lipases hydrolyse dietary fats.

Q: Which enzyme begins starch breakdown in saliva?
A) Lipase  B) Insulin  C) Amylase*  D) Collagen
Why: Salivary amylase starts starch digestion.

Q: What is a protease?
A) An oxygen carrier  B) A fat store  C) A mineral salt  D) A protein-digesting enzyme*
Why: Proteases break proteins into smaller peptides or amino acids.

Q: Why must many food molecules be digested?
A) To allow absorption across the gut lining*  B) To create oxygen  C) To form red cells in the stomach  D) To stop all gut movement
Why: Smaller molecules can be transported across the intestinal barrier.
Source: [https://training.seer.cancer.gov/anatomy/digestive/?view=searchengine](https://training.seer.cancer.gov/anatomy/digestive/?view=searchengine)

Q: Which secretion helps neutralise acidic chyme?
A) Haemoglobin  B) Bicarbonate*  C) Melanin  D) Keratin
Why: Bicarbonate buffers acid arriving from the stomach.

Q: What is the main role of hydrochloric acid in the stomach?
A) Emulsifies every fat droplet  B) Absorbs all amino acids  C) Creates conditions for gastric enzyme activity*  D) Produces bile
Why: Acid supports the activation and activity of gastric proteases.

Q: Why does the small intestine have folds and villi?
A) They make the wall impermeable  B) They replace blood vessels  C) They stop enzyme action  D) They enlarge the absorbing surface*
Why: Greater surface area supports efficient nutrient uptake.

Q: Which route carries many absorbed sugars first to the liver?
A) Hepatic portal circulation*  B) Pulmonary circulation  C) Coronary circulation  D) Airway ventilation
Why: Portal blood carries many absorbed nutrients to the liver.

Q: Which vessels inside villi take up many dietary fats?
A) Bronchioles  B) Lacteals*  C) Coronary arteries  D) Ureters
Why: Lacteals carry fat-rich lymph from intestinal villi.

Q: Which pairing is correct?
A) Gall bladder — bile production  B) Rectum — most nutrient absorption  C) Pancreas — digestive enzyme secretion*  D) Oesophagus — urine storage
Why: Pancreatic juice supplies digestive enzymes.

Q: Which statement about bile is correct?
A) It is a protease  B) It is a red cell  C) It is a carbohydrate  D) It assists digestion but is not an enzyme*
Why: Bile salts aid fat dispersion without enzymatically hydrolysing it.

Q: What does a sphincter do in the digestive tract?
A) Controls passage between regions*  B) Makes all bile  C) Transports oxygen  D) Produces tooth enamel
Why: Sphincter contraction and relaxation regulate movement through openings.

Q: What separates the stomach from the duodenum?
A) Anal sphincter  B) Pyloric sphincter*  C) Iris  D) Mitral valve
Why: The pyloric sphincter controls chyme leaving the stomach.

Q: What is the main purpose of intestinal peristalsis?
A) Making haemoglobin  B) Transporting air into alveoli  C) Moving contents along the tract*  D) Filtering blood into urine
Why: Peristaltic waves propel gut contents.

Q: Which process uses water to split food molecules?
A) Photosynthesis  B) Blood clotting  C) Ossification  D) Hydrolysis*
Why: Hydrolysis splits molecules by adding water.
Source: [https://training.seer.cancer.gov/anatomy/digestive/?view=searchengine](https://training.seer.cancer.gov/anatomy/digestive/?view=searchengine)

Q: What is a bolus?
A) A lump of chewed food mixed with saliva*  B) Stored urine  C) An alveolar air pocket  D) A blood clot
Why: Chewing and saliva form food into a bolus.

Q: Why does the colon absorb water?
A) It turns all fibre into glucose  B) It makes the remaining contents more solid*  C) It produces oxygen  D) It converts bile into blood
Why: Removing water helps form solid faeces.

Q: Which function belongs to gut bacteria?
A) Making tooth enamel  B) Pumping blood  C) Producing some vitamins*  D) Replacing all digestive enzymes
Why: Some intestinal bacteria make vitamins including vitamin K.
Source: [https://www.niddk.nih.gov/health-information/digestive-diseases/digestive-system-how-it-works](https://www.niddk.nih.gov/health-information/digestive-diseases/digestive-system-how-it-works)

Q: Which distinction between digestion and egestion is correct?
A) Egestion makes enzymes  B) Digestion removes urine  C) Both mean absorption  D) Egestion removes undigested material*
Why: Egestion is the elimination of material not absorbed from the gut.

# Science · Adult · Food and digestion

Q: What benefit follows when bile divides fat into small droplets?
A) Fat becomes protein  B) Greater surface area for lipase*  C) Enzymes become unnecessary  D) Absorption stops
Why: Smaller droplets expose more surface to enzyme action.

Q: Which digestive enzyme catalyses fat breakdown?
A) Amylase  B) Pepsin  C) Lipase*  D) Haemoglobin
Why: Lipases hydrolyse dietary fats.

Q: Which salivary enzyme acts on starch?
A) Lipase  B) Insulin  C) Collagen  D) Amylase*
Why: Salivary amylase starts starch digestion.

Q: Which enzyme class hydrolyses proteins?
A) A protein-digesting enzyme*  B) An oxygen carrier  C) A fat store  D) A mineral salt
Why: Proteases break proteins into smaller peptides or amino acids.

Q: Why are large dietary molecules usually broken into smaller units?
A) To create oxygen  B) To allow absorption across the gut lining*  C) To form red cells in the stomach  D) To stop all gut movement
Why: Smaller molecules can be transported across the intestinal barrier.

Q: What component of pancreatic juice reduces acidity in the duodenum?
A) Haemoglobin  B) Melanin  C) Bicarbonate*  D) Keratin
Why: Bicarbonate buffers acid arriving from the stomach.

Q: How does gastric acid assist protein digestion?
A) Emulsifies every fat droplet  B) Absorbs all amino acids  C) Produces bile  D) Creates conditions for gastric enzyme activity*
Why: Acid supports the activation and activity of gastric proteases.

Q: How do folds, villi and microvilli support absorption?
A) They enlarge the absorbing surface*  B) They make the wall impermeable  C) They replace blood vessels  D) They stop enzyme action
Why: Greater surface area supports efficient nutrient uptake.

Q: Which circulation delivers absorbed glucose from the intestine to the liver?
A) Pulmonary circulation  B) Hepatic portal circulation*  C) Coronary circulation  D) Airway ventilation
Why: Portal blood carries many absorbed nutrients to the liver.

Q: Where do many long-chain dietary fats enter after intestinal packaging?
A) Bronchioles  B) Coronary arteries  C) Lacteals*  D) Ureters
Why: Lacteals carry fat-rich lymph from intestinal villi.

Q: Which organ-function pairing is accurate?
A) Gall bladder — bile production  B) Rectum — most nutrient absorption  C) Oesophagus — urine storage  D) Pancreas — digestive enzyme secretion*
Why: Pancreatic juice supplies digestive enzymes.

Q: How should bile be classified in fat digestion?
A) It assists digestion but is not an enzyme*  B) It is a protease  C) It is a red cell  D) It is a carbohydrate
Why: Bile salts aid fat dispersion without enzymatically hydrolysing it.

Q: What is the function of a ring of muscle at a gut opening?
A) Makes all bile  B) Controls passage between regions*  C) Transports oxygen  D) Produces tooth enamel
Why: Sphincter contraction and relaxation regulate movement through openings.

Q: Which sphincter regulates stomach emptying into the small intestine?
A) Anal sphincter  B) Iris  C) Pyloric sphincter*  D) Mitral valve
Why: The pyloric sphincter controls chyme leaving the stomach.

Q: Which function is performed by intestinal peristalsis?
A) Making haemoglobin  B) Transporting air into alveoli  C) Filtering blood into urine  D) Moving contents along the tract*
Why: Peristaltic waves propel gut contents.

Q: Which chemical reaction underlies much enzymatic digestion?
A) Hydrolysis*  B) Photosynthesis  C) Blood clotting  D) Ossification
Why: Hydrolysis splits molecules by adding water.
Source: [https://training.seer.cancer.gov/anatomy/digestive/?view=searchengine](https://training.seer.cancer.gov/anatomy/digestive/?view=searchengine)

Q: What name describes a swallowed mass of chewed food?
A) Stored urine  B) A lump of chewed food mixed with saliva*  C) An alveolar air pocket  D) A blood clot
Why: Chewing and saliva form food into a bolus.

Q: What effect does colonic water absorption have on gut contents?
A) It turns all fibre into glucose  B) It produces oxygen  C) It makes the remaining contents more solid*  D) It converts bile into blood
Why: Removing water helps form solid faeces.

Q: Which contribution can intestinal microbes make to nutrition?
A) Making tooth enamel  B) Pumping blood  C) Replacing all digestive enzymes  D) Producing some vitamins*
Why: Some intestinal bacteria make vitamins including vitamin K.

Q: How does egestion differ from chemical digestion?
A) Egestion removes undigested material*  B) Egestion makes enzymes  C) Digestion removes urine  D) Both mean absorption
Why: Egestion is the elimination of material not absorbed from the gut.

# Science · Ages 4–5 · Bones and movement

Q: What is the framework of bones inside you called?
A) Stomach  B) Skeleton*  C) Skin  D) Tongue
Why: The skeleton supports the body.
Source: [https://www.healthdirect.gov.au/anatomy/bones-muscles-and-joints](https://www.healthdirect.gov.au/anatomy/bones-muscles-and-joints)

Q: What hard parts are inside your arms and legs?
A) Feathers  B) Leaves  C) Bones*  D) Wires
Why: Bones provide firm support inside the limbs.

Q: What protects your brain?
A) Heel  B) Elbow  C) Wrist  D) Skull*
Why: The skull protects the brain.

Q: What protects your heart and lungs?
A) Rib cage*  B) Kneecap  C) Ankle  D) Jaw
Why: Ribs form a protective cage around chest organs.

Q: Which part bends in the middle of your arm?
A) Ankle  B) Elbow*  C) Hip  D) Knee
Why: The elbow joins the upper arm and forearm.

Q: Which part bends in the middle of your leg?
A) Wrist  B) Elbow  C) Knee*  D) Shoulder
Why: The knee allows the leg to bend.

Q: Which part joins your hand to your arm?
A) Knee  B) Hip  C) Ankle  D) Wrist*
Why: The wrist connects the hand and forearm.

Q: Which part joins your foot to your leg?
A) Ankle*  B) Elbow  C) Shoulder  D) Wrist
Why: The ankle connects the lower leg and foot.

Q: Which body parts help pull your bones to move?
A) Hair  B) Muscles*  C) Nails  D) Teeth
Why: Muscles pull on bones to produce movement.
Source: [https://www.healthdirect.gov.au/anatomy/bones-muscles-and-joints](https://www.healthdirect.gov.au/anatomy/bones-muscles-and-joints)

Q: Where are your finger bones?
A) Feet  B) Ears  C) Hands*  D) Nose
Why: Finger bones form part of each hand.

Q: Where are your toe bones?
A) Hands  B) Cheeks  C) Elbows  D) Feet*
Why: Toe bones form part of each foot.

Q: Which action uses your leg muscles?
A) Jumping*  B) Blinking  C) Chewing  D) Smelling
Why: Leg muscles help lift the body during a jump.

Q: Which action uses your arm muscles?
A) Hearing a bell  B) Lifting a toy*  C) Smelling a flower  D) Tasting soup
Why: Arm muscles pull on bones when you lift.

Q: Which part of your face moves when you chew?
A) Forehead  B) Skull roof  C) Lower jaw*  D) Nose tip
Why: The lower jaw moves during chewing.

Q: What holds your head above your shoulders?
A) Ankle  B) Heel  C) Wrist  D) Neck*
Why: The neck supports and allows movement of the head.

Q: What is your backbone also called?
A) Spine*  B) Rib  C) Jaw  D) Thumb

Q: Which part joins your arm to your body?
A) Ankle  B) Shoulder*  C) Wrist  D) Knee
Why: The shoulder allows the upper arm to move.

Q: What do bones help your body keep?
A) Feathers  B) Sunlight  C) Shape and support*  D) Scales
Why: The skeleton gives the body structure.

Q: What happens to many of your bones as you grow?
A) They turn into air  B) They all disappear  C) They become leaves  D) They become longer and larger*
Why: Bones grow as a child develops.

Q: Which activity helps keep muscles strong?
A) Active play*  B) Never moving  C) Only sitting still  D) Avoiding every game
Why: Using muscles during activity helps strengthen them.

Q: Which movable part carries the lower teeth?
A) Forehead  B) Skull roof  C) Nose tip  D) Lower jaw*

Q: Which part between the head and shoulders supports the head?
A) Neck*  B) Ankle  C) Heel  D) Wrist

Q: What name is used for the column of bones down your back?

A) Ankle  B) Wrist  C) Shoulder*  D) Knee

# Science · Ages 9–11 · Bones and movement

Q: How many bones are usually counted in an adult skeleton?
A) 106  B) 206*  C) 306  D) 406
Why: The usual adult skeletal count is 206.

Q: What is a joint?
A) A type of blood cell  B) A stomach enzyme  C) A place where bones meet*  D) An air sac
Why: Joints connect parts of the skeleton.

Q: What connects muscle to bone?
A) Ligament  B) Retina  C) Bronchus  D) Tendon*
Why: Tendons attach muscles to bones.
Source: [https://www.healthdirect.gov.au/anatomy/bones-muscles-and-joints](https://www.healthdirect.gov.au/anatomy/bones-muscles-and-joints)

Q: What connects bone to bone at many joints?
A) Ligaments*  B) Tendons  C) Neurons  D) Alveoli
Why: Ligaments help hold bones together.

Q: What cushions the ends of bones at a movable joint?
A) Enamel  B) Cartilage*  C) Hair  D) Skin pigment
Why: Cartilage cushions surfaces and reduces friction.

Q: Which joint type is found at the elbow?
A) Ball-and-socket  B) Fixed skull joint  C) Hinge*  D) Tooth socket
Why: The main elbow movement is hinge-like.

Q: Which joint type is found at the hip?
A) Hinge  B) Fixed suture  C) Tooth socket  D) Ball-and-socket*
Why: A rounded head fits into a cup-shaped socket.

Q: What is the thigh bone called?
A) Femur*  B) Humerus  C) Radius  D) Ulna
Why: The femur is the thigh bone.

Q: What is the upper arm bone called?
A) Femur  B) Humerus*  C) Tibia  D) Fibula
Why: The humerus forms the upper arm.

Q: What is the kneecap called?
A) Scapula  B) Sternum  C) Patella*  D) Clavicle
Why: The patella is the kneecap.

Q: What is the breastbone called?
A) Patella  B) Femur  C) Ulna  D) Sternum*
Why: The sternum lies at the front of the chest.

Q: What is the collarbone called?
A) Clavicle*  B) Tibia  C) Radius  D) Mandible
Why: The clavicle is the collarbone.

Q: Where are new blood cells produced in bones?
A) Joint cartilage  B) Red bone marrow*  C) Tooth enamel  D) Tendon
Why: Red marrow produces blood cells.

Q: What mineral helps make bones hard?
A) Helium  B) Mercury  C) Calcium*  D) Neon
Why: Calcium salts contribute to bone strength.
Source: [https://health.nih.gov/health-topics-a-z/bone-health](https://health.nih.gov/health-topics-a-z/bone-health)

Q: Are bones living tissue?
A) No, they are dead stone  B) No, they contain only air  C) Only teeth are alive  D) Yes, with living cells and a blood supply*
Why: Bone is living tissue that changes throughout life.
Source: [https://health.nih.gov/health-topics-a-z/bone-health](https://health.nih.gov/health-topics-a-z/bone-health)

Q: What happens when a skeletal muscle contracts?
A) It develops tension and can shorten*  B) It pushes a bone directly  C) It turns into cartilage  D) It becomes a nerve
Why: Contracting muscles pull through their tendons.

Q: Why do muscles work in opposing pairs?
A) Bones cannot move  B) Muscles pull rather than push*  C) Tendons digest food  D) Joints make their own force
Why: Opposing muscles pull bones in different directions.

Q: Which type of muscle forms the heart?
A) Skeletal muscle  B) Smooth cartilage  C) Cardiac muscle*  D) Bone marrow
Why: Cardiac muscle is specialised heart muscle.

Q: Which type of muscle is found in the gut wall?
A) Cardiac muscle  B) Enamel  C) Compact bone  D) Smooth muscle*
Why: Smooth muscle works without conscious control.

Q: What is a fracture?
A) A break in a bone*  B) A joint lubricant  C) A nerve signal  D) A muscle enzyme
Why: A fracture is a crack or break in bone.
Source: [https://health.nih.gov/health-topics-a-z/bone-health](https://health.nih.gov/health-topics-a-z/bone-health)

# Science · Ages 15–16 · Bones and movement

Q: What is the main role of osteoblasts?
A) Bone resorption  B) Bone formation*  C) Oxygen transport  D) Insulin release
Why: Osteoblasts build the bone matrix.
Source: [https://training.seer.cancer.gov/anatomy/skeletal/growth.html](https://training.seer.cancer.gov/anatomy/skeletal/growth.html)

Q: What is the main role of osteoclasts?
A) Antibody production  B) Cartilage lubrication  C) Bone resorption*  D) Muscle contraction
Why: Osteoclasts break down bone tissue.
Source: [https://training.seer.cancer.gov/anatomy/skeletal/growth.html](https://training.seer.cancer.gov/anatomy/skeletal/growth.html)

Q: Which protein gives bone part of its flexibility?
A) Haemoglobin  B) Insulin  C) Amylase  D) Collagen*
Why: Collagen forms a flexible framework within bone.

Q: What is compact bone?
A) Dense, hard bone tissue*  B) A tendon sheath  C) A joint space  D) A nerve bundle
Why: Compact bone contributes strength to the skeleton.
Source: [https://health.nih.gov/health-topics-a-z/bone-health](https://health.nih.gov/health-topics-a-z/bone-health)

Q: What is spongy bone?
A) Tooth enamel  B) Trabecular bone*  C) Articular fluid  D) Skeletal muscle
Why: Trabecular bone has a lattice-like internal structure.
Source: [https://health.nih.gov/health-topics-a-z/bone-health](https://health.nih.gov/health-topics-a-z/bone-health)

Q: What covers the outer surface of most bones?
A) Retina  B) Pleura  C) Periosteum*  D) Peritoneum
Why: The periosteum contains blood vessels, nerves and bone-related cells.

Q: Which structure permits lengthwise growth in a child’s long bone?
A) Joint capsule  B) Tendon insertion only  C) Central canal only  D) Growth plate*
Why: Cartilage at growth plates is replaced by bone.
Source: [https://training.seer.cancer.gov/anatomy/skeletal/growth.html](https://training.seer.cancer.gov/anatomy/skeletal/growth.html)

Q: What is synovial fluid’s main mechanical role?
A) Reducing friction*  B) Carrying air  C) Making insulin  D) Breaking down starch
Why: Synovial fluid lubricates moving joint surfaces.
Source: [https://www.healthdirect.gov.au/anatomy/bones-muscles-and-joints](https://www.healthdirect.gov.au/anatomy/bones-muscles-and-joints)

Q: Which structure stabilises a synovial joint by joining bones?
A) Axon  B) Ligament*  C) Lacteal  D) Bronchiole
Why: Ligaments support the joint and guide movement.

Q: Which structure transmits force from a muscle to bone?
A) Retina  B) Vein valve  C) Tendon*  D) Eardrum
Why: Tendons transmit muscle tension to bone.
Source: [https://www.healthdirect.gov.au/anatomy/bones-muscles-and-joints](https://www.healthdirect.gov.au/anatomy/bones-muscles-and-joints)

Q: What is an antagonistic muscle pair?
A) Two bones fused together  B) Two arteries carrying blood  C) Identical sensory receptors  D) Muscles acting in opposite directions*
Why: One muscle’s action opposes that of the other.

Q: What movement decreases the angle at a joint?
A) Flexion*  B) Extension  C) Abduction  D) Rotation
Why: Flexion reduces the angle between adjacent limb segments.

Q: What movement increases the angle at a joint?
A) Flexion  B) Extension*  C) Adduction  D) Pronation
Why: Extension increases the angle between adjacent limb segments.

Q: What is abduction?
A) Movement towards the midline  B) Bending a joint  C) Movement away from the midline*  D) Turning the palm down
Why: Abduction moves a body part away from the midline.

Q: What is adduction?
A) Movement away from the midline  B) Straightening a joint  C) Turning the palm up  D) Movement towards the midline*
Why: Adduction brings a body part towards the midline.

Q: Which fibres slide past each other during muscle contraction?
A) Actin and myosin*  B) Insulin and glucagon  C) Amylase and starch  D) Collagen and enamel
Why: Actin–myosin interactions generate muscle force.

Q: What is a motor unit?
A) A bone and a ligament  B) A motor neuron and the muscle fibres it supplies*  C) Two joints and a tendon  D) An artery and a vein
Why: A motor neuron activates its connected muscle fibres.

Q: What is the neuromuscular junction?
A) A bone-growth plate  B) A joint cavity  C) A nerve-to-muscle synapse*  D) A capillary valve
Why: The junction transfers a nerve signal to muscle.

Q: Which part of the skeleton includes the skull and spine?
A) Appendicular skeleton  B) Peripheral nervous system  C) Endocrine system  D) Axial skeleton*
Why: The axial skeleton forms the body’s central framework.

Q: Which part of the skeleton includes the limbs and their girdles?
A) Appendicular skeleton*  B) Axial skeleton  C) Central nervous system  D) Respiratory system
Why: The appendicular skeleton supports limb movement.

# Science · Adult · Bones and movement

Q: Which bone cells lay down new bone tissue?
A) Bone resorption  B) Oxygen transport  C) Bone formation*  D) Insulin release
Why: Osteoblasts build the bone matrix.
Source: [https://training.seer.cancer.gov/anatomy/skeletal/growth.html](https://training.seer.cancer.gov/anatomy/skeletal/growth.html)

Q: Which cells remove bone during remodelling?
A) Antibody production  B) Cartilage lubrication  C) Muscle contraction  D) Bone resorption*
Why: Osteoclasts break down bone tissue.
Source: [https://training.seer.cancer.gov/anatomy/skeletal/growth.html](https://training.seer.cancer.gov/anatomy/skeletal/growth.html)

Q: Which organic component helps bone resist tensile forces?
A) Collagen*  B) Haemoglobin  C) Insulin  D) Amylase
Why: Collagen forms a flexible framework within bone.

Q: Which bone tissue forms a dense outer layer?
A) A tendon sheath  B) Dense, hard bone tissue*  C) A joint space  D) A nerve bundle
Why: Compact bone contributes strength to the skeleton.
Source: [https://health.nih.gov/health-topics-a-z/bone-health](https://health.nih.gov/health-topics-a-z/bone-health)

Q: Which bone tissue contains a network of supporting struts?
A) Tooth enamel  B) Articular fluid  C) Trabecular bone*  D) Skeletal muscle
Why: Trabecular bone has a lattice-like internal structure.

Q: Which connective tissue membrane surrounds bone except at joint surfaces?
A) Retina  B) Pleura  C) Peritoneum  D) Periosteum*
Why: The periosteum contains blood vessels, nerves and bone-related cells.
Source: [https://health.nih.gov/health-topics-a-z/bone-health](https://health.nih.gov/health-topics-a-z/bone-health)

Q: Where does a growing long bone increase in length?
A) Growth plate*  B) Joint capsule  C) Tendon insertion only  D) Central canal only
Why: Cartilage at growth plates is replaced by bone.
Source: [https://training.seer.cancer.gov/anatomy/skeletal/growth.html](https://training.seer.cancer.gov/anatomy/skeletal/growth.html)

Q: Why does a synovial joint contain lubricating fluid?
A) Carrying air  B) Reducing friction*  C) Making insulin  D) Breaking down starch
Why: Synovial fluid lubricates moving joint surfaces.
Source: [https://www.healthdirect.gov.au/anatomy/bones-muscles-and-joints](https://www.healthdirect.gov.au/anatomy/bones-muscles-and-joints)

Q: Which tissue helps restrict excessive joint movement?
A) Axon  B) Lacteal  C) Ligament*  D) Bronchiole
Why: Ligaments support the joint and guide movement.

Q: A muscle contracts but must move a bone: which tissue transfers its force?
A) Retina  B) Vein valve  C) Eardrum  D) Tendon*
Why: Tendons transmit muscle tension to bone.
Source: [https://www.healthdirect.gov.au/anatomy/bones-muscles-and-joints](https://www.healthdirect.gov.au/anatomy/bones-muscles-and-joints)

Q: How are muscles that produce opposite movements described?
A) Muscles acting in opposite directions*  B) Two bones fused together  C) Two arteries carrying blood  D) Identical sensory receptors
Why: One muscle’s action opposes that of the other.

Q: Which term describes bending the elbow to bring hand towards shoulder?
A) Extension  B) Flexion*  C) Abduction  D) Rotation
Why: Flexion reduces the angle between adjacent limb segments.

Q: Which term describes straightening a bent elbow?
A) Flexion  B) Adduction  C) Extension*  D) Pronation
Why: Extension increases the angle between adjacent limb segments.

Q: Which term describes moving a limb away from the body’s midline?
A) Movement towards the midline  B) Bending a joint  C) Turning the palm down  D) Movement away from the midline*
Why: Abduction moves a body part away from the midline.

Q: Which term describes bringing an outstretched arm back towards the body?
A) Movement towards the midline*  B) Movement away from the midline  C) Straightening a joint  D) Turning the palm up
Why: Adduction brings a body part towards the midline.

Q: Which proteins interact in the sliding-filament mechanism?
A) Insulin and glucagon  B) Actin and myosin*  C) Amylase and starch  D) Collagen and enamel
Why: Actin–myosin interactions generate muscle force.

Q: Which combination forms one functional unit of skeletal-muscle activation?
A) A bone and a ligament  B) Two joints and a tendon  C) A motor neuron and the muscle fibres it supplies*  D) An artery and a vein
Why: A motor neuron activates its connected muscle fibres.

Q: Where does a motor neuron communicate with a skeletal-muscle fibre?
A) A bone-growth plate  B) A joint cavity  C) A capillary valve  D) A nerve-to-muscle synapse*
Why: The junction transfers a nerve signal to muscle.

Q: To which division do the vertebral column and rib cage belong?
A) Axial skeleton*  B) Appendicular skeleton  C) Peripheral nervous system  D) Endocrine system
Why: The axial skeleton forms the body’s central framework.

Q: To which division do the arms, legs, shoulder and pelvic girdles belong?
A) Axial skeleton  B) Appendicular skeleton*  C) Central nervous system  D) Respiratory system
Why: The appendicular skeleton supports limb movement.

Why: Eyes detect light.

Q: Which part helps you taste food?

A) Sight*  B) Hearing  C) Taste  D) Smell

Q: Which sense tells you a lemon tastes sour?

Q: Which sense helps you notice a flower’s perfume?

Q: What covers most of your body and helps you feel touch?

Q: Which taste is usually found in a little sugar?

Q: Which taste does a little table salt give?

Q: Which taste is often found in lemon juice?
A) Sour*  B) Sweet  C) Salty  D) Umami
Why: Acids in lemon juice give a sour taste.

Q: Which sense helps tell that a pebble is smooth?
A) Smell  B) Touch*  C) Hearing  D) Taste
Why: Skin receptors help detect surface texture.

Q: Which sense helps you recognise a friend’s voice?
A) Taste  B) Touch  C) Hearing*  D) Smell

Q: What carries hearing signals to the brain?

Q: Which cells help detect vibrations inside the cochlea?
A) Hair cells*  B) Red blood cells  C) Bone cells  D) Fat cells

Q: What helps your inner ear detect head movement?
A) Taste buds  B) Semicircular canals*  C) Villi  D) Alveoli

Q: Which skin structures detect touch?
A) Digestive glands  B) Air sacs  C) Sensory receptors*  D) Heart valves
Why: Receptors convert stimuli into signals for the nervous system.

Q: Which two senses work together to create much of food flavour?
A) Hearing and balance  B) Sight and balance  C) Touch and hearing only  D) Taste and smell*
Why: Smell adds much to the flavour of food.

Q: Where are smell-detecting cells found?
A) High inside the nose*  B) Inside the kneecap  C) On tooth enamel  D) In the heel
Why: Olfactory cells detect odour molecules in the nose.

Q: What are taste buds made up of?
A) Tiny bones  B) Groups of sensory cells*  C) Air pockets  D) Blood clots
Why: Taste buds contain specialised taste receptor cells.

Q: What is umami often described as?

# Science · Ages 15–16 · The senses

Q: Which photoreceptors are most useful in dim light?
A) Cones  B) Hair cells  C) Rods*  D) Osteocytes
Why: Rods are specialised for low-light vision.

Q: Which photoreceptors support colour vision?
A) Rods only  B) Platelets  C) Taste cells  D) Cones*
Why: Different cone types support colour discrimination.

Q: What is accommodation in the eye?
A) Changing lens shape*  B) Changing ear pressure  C) Making more retinal blood  D) Moving the skull
Why: Lens shape changes to focus light on the retina.

Q: What part of the eye has no photoreceptors where the optic nerve exits?
A) Fovea  B) Optic disc*  C) Iris  D) Cornea
Why: The optic disc has no rods or cones.

Q: Which retinal region supports very sharp central vision?
A) Optic disc  B) Corneal edge  C) Fovea*  D) Pupil
Why: The fovea supports high-resolution central vision.

Q: What are the middle-ear ossicles called?
A) Radius, ulna and humerus  B) Iris, lens and retina  C) Tibia, fibula and femur  D) Malleus, incus and stapes*
Why: The ossicles transmit vibrations towards the inner ear.
Source: [https://www.nidcd.nih.gov/health/how-do-we-hear](https://www.nidcd.nih.gov/health/how-do-we-hear)

Q: What is the main role of the Eustachian tube?
A) Equalising pressure across the eardrum*  B) Detecting light  C) Producing saliva  D) Transporting oxygen in blood
Why: The tube helps balance middle-ear pressure.

Q: What is sensory transduction?
A) Production of bone marrow  B) Conversion of a stimulus into an electrical signal*  C) Breaking protein into amino acids  D) Pumping blood into arteries
Why: Receptors convert stimulus energy into cellular signals.

Q: What is sensory adaptation?
A) Permanent loss of every receptor  B) A change from smell to vision  C) Reduced response to a continuing stimulus*  D) Increased blood clotting
Why: Responses often decrease during sustained stimulation.

Q: Which senses are chemical senses?
A) Sight and hearing  B) Balance and sight  C) Hearing and touch  D) Taste and smell*
Why: Taste and smell respond to chemical substances.
Source: [https://www.nidcd.nih.gov/health/smell-disorders](https://www.nidcd.nih.gov/health/smell-disorders)

Q: What is the olfactory bulb?
A) A structure processing smell signals*  B) A digestive gland  C) A bone in the ear  D) A chamber of the heart
Why: Olfactory input is relayed through the olfactory bulb.

Q: Why does a blocked nose reduce food flavour?
A) All ability to detect sweetness  B) Much of the smell contribution*  C) All tongue movement  D) All saliva production
Why: Aromas from food contribute strongly to flavour.
Source: [https://www.nidcd.nih.gov/health/smell-disorders](https://www.nidcd.nih.gov/health/smell-disorders)

Q: Is the traditional tongue map of separate taste zones accurate?
A) Yes, sweetness exists only at the tip  B) Yes, bitterness exists only on the lips  C) No, taste qualities can be detected across taste-bearing regions*  D) Yes, salt is detected only by teeth
Why: Taste qualities are not confined to separate mapped zones.

Q: Which system helps sense body-part position without looking?
A) Olfaction  B) Accommodation  C) Emulsification  D) Proprioception*
Why: Proprioceptors report muscle length and joint-related movement.

Q: Which receptors detect potentially damaging stimuli?
A) Nociceptors*  B) Photoreceptors  C) Olfactory receptors  D) Taste receptors
Why: Nociceptors respond to potentially harmful mechanical, thermal or chemical stimuli.

Q: Which receptors detect temperature changes?
A) Osteoblasts  B) Thermoreceptors*  C) Platelets  D) Hepatocytes
Why: Thermoreceptors respond to temperature.

Q: Which sensory system detects angular head acceleration?
A) Cochlear tip only  B) Eustachian tube  C) Semicircular canals*  D) Eardrum only
Why: Fluid movement in the semicircular canals signals rotation.

Q: What mainly determines the pitch we perceive?
A) Blood pressure  B) Eye colour  C) Body temperature  D) Frequency*
Why: Higher frequencies are generally heard as higher pitches.

Q: What mainly determines sound intensity?
A) Amplitude*  B) Taste receptor number  C) Iris colour  D) Lens thickness
Why: Larger wave amplitudes correspond to greater sound intensity.

Q: Which process lets both eyes contribute to depth judgement?
A) Identical sounds in both ears  B) Differences between the two retinal images*  C) Taste-bud arrangement  D) Nasal airflow alone
Why: The brain compares the slightly different views from both eyes.

Why: Receptors convert stimulus energy into cellular signals.

# Science · Ages 9–11 · Brain and nerves

Q: What are the brain and spinal cord together called?
A) Digestive system  B) Endocrine system  C) Lymphatic system  D) Central nervous system*
Why: The CNS consists of brain and spinal cord.

Q: What are the nerves outside the brain and spinal cord called?
A) Peripheral nervous system*  B) Central skeleton  C) Respiratory system  D) Digestive tract
Why: Peripheral nerves connect the CNS with the body.

Q: What is a neuron?
A) A blood cell  B) A nerve cell*  C) A bone mineral  D) A digestive enzyme
Why: Neurons receive and transmit information.
Source: [https://www.training.seer.cancer.gov/anatomy/cells_tissues_membranes/tissues/nervous.html](https://www.training.seer.cancer.gov/anatomy/cells_tissues_membranes/tissues/nervous.html)

Q: What does a sensory neuron carry?
A) Only from the stomach to the liver  B) From arteries to veins  C) From receptors towards the CNS*  D) Only out of the body
Why: Sensory neurons bring information towards the CNS.

Q: What does a motor neuron carry?
A) Oxygen molecules  B) Bile droplets  C) Pieces of food  D) Instructions from the nervous system*
Why: Motor neurons activate muscles.

Q: What is a reflex?
A) A rapid automatic response to a stimulus*  B) A deliberately written plan  C) A type of bone growth  D) A hormone gland
Why: Reflexes happen without a conscious decision first.

Q: Which structure can coordinate a simple withdrawal reflex?
A) Stomach  B) Spinal cord*  C) Liver  D) Gall bladder
Why: Spinal circuits can coordinate rapid withdrawal.

Q: Which part of a neuron carries signals away from its cell body?
A) Dendrite  B) Nucleus  C) Axon*  D) Rib
Why: The axon carries signals onwards.
Source: [https://www.training.seer.cancer.gov/anatomy/cells_tissues_membranes/tissues/nervous.html](https://www.training.seer.cancer.gov/anatomy/cells_tissues_membranes/tissues/nervous.html)

Q: Which branched parts usually receive input to a neuron?
A) Tendons  B) Villi  C) Alveoli  D) Dendrites*
Why: Dendrites receive signals from other cells.
Source: [https://www.training.seer.cancer.gov/anatomy/cells_tissues_membranes/tissues/nervous.html](https://www.training.seer.cancer.gov/anatomy/cells_tissues_membranes/tissues/nervous.html)

Q: What is a synapse?
A) A communication junction*  B) A bone cavity  C) A heart chamber  D) A digestive valve
Why: Synapses transfer signals between cells.

Q: What is myelin?
A) A stomach acid  B) An insulating sheath*  C) A bone mineral  D) An eye pigment
Why: Myelin helps signals travel efficiently.
Source: [https://training.seer.cancer.gov/anatomy/nervous/tissue.html](https://training.seer.cancer.gov/anatomy/nervous/tissue.html)

Q: Which brain part helps coordinate movement?
A) Retina  B) Pancreas  C) Cerebellum*  D) Thyroid
Why: The cerebellum helps refine movement and balance.

Q: Which large brain region supports thinking and conscious activity?
A) Cochlea  B) Larynx  C) Colon  D) Cerebrum*
Why: The cerebrum supports complex thinking and perception.

Q: Which brain region links to the spinal cord?
A) Brainstem*  B) Iris  C) Duodenum  D) Patella
Why: The brainstem connects with the spinal cord.

Q: What do we call the brain’s outer folded layer?
A) Bone marrow  B) Cerebral cortex*  C) Joint capsule  D) Gastric lining
Why: The cortex is a thin outer layer of the cerebrum.

Q: How many cerebral hemispheres are there?
A) One  B) Three  C) Two*  D) Five
Why: The cerebrum has left and right hemispheres.

Q: Which bridge links the cerebral hemispheres?
A) Achilles tendon  B) Pulmonary artery  C) Optic lens  D) Corpus callosum*
Why: The corpus callosum allows communication between hemispheres.

Q: What is a stimulus?
A) A detectable change*  B) A red blood cell  C) A type of tooth  D) An intestinal section
Why: Receptors respond to changes such as light or pressure.

Q: Which system helps control automatic functions such as gut movement?
A) Appendicular skeleton  B) Autonomic nervous system*  C) Digestive enzymes  D) Voluntary muscle only
Why: Autonomic pathways regulate internal organs.

Q: What is the main purpose of nervous coordination?
A) To make all hormones in the skin  B) To turn blood into bone  C) To organise appropriate responses*  D) To replace digestion
Why: Coordination links incoming information with suitable actions.

# Science · Ages 15–16 · Brain and nerves

Q: What is an action potential?
A) A bone contraction  B) An antibody  C) A digestive droplet  D) A rapid change in membrane voltage*
Why: Action potentials carry information along nerve fibres.

Q: What is a neurotransmitter?
A) A chemical messenger released by a neuron*  B) A blood-clotting cell  C) A bone mineral  D) A lung air sac
Why: Neurotransmitters bind to receptors on another cell.

Q: What is the synaptic cleft?
A) A bone-growth zone  B) The gap between communicating cells*  C) A heart chamber  D) A gland duct
Why: Neurotransmitter diffuses across the synaptic cleft.

Q: Why is myelin useful?
A) It digests neurotransmitters in the stomach  B) It produces every action potential  C) It speeds electrical signal conduction*  D) It blocks all communication
Why: Myelin enables rapid conduction between nodes.

Q: What is saltatory conduction?
A) Movement through red blood cells  B) Diffusion through bone  C) Flow through a gland duct  D) Propagation between nodes of Ranvier*
Why: Action potentials regenerate at gaps in the myelin sheath.

Q: Which cells form myelin in the peripheral nervous system?
A) Schwann cells*  B) Osteoblasts  C) Platelets  D) Hepatocytes
Why: Schwann cells myelinate peripheral nerve fibres.
Source: [https://training.seer.cancer.gov/anatomy/nervous/tissue.html](https://training.seer.cancer.gov/anatomy/nervous/tissue.html)

Q: Which cells form myelin in the central nervous system?
A) Red blood cells  B) Oligodendrocytes*  C) Taste cells  D) Osteoclasts
Why: Oligodendrocytes myelinate CNS axons.

Q: What is an effector?
A) A stimulus  B) A synaptic gap  C) A muscle or gland*  D) A sensory receptor only
Why: Effectors act in response to nervous signals.

Q: What is the usual sequence in a simple reflex arc?
A) Muscle → stomach → retina  B) Receptor → vein → liver  C) Bone → tendon → lens  D) Receptor → sensory neuron → CNS → motor neuron → muscle*
Why: The arc links detection to a motor response.

Q: What does the sympathetic nervous system generally prepare the body for?
A) Rapid action during stress*  B) Deep digestion only  C) Bone formation only  D) Colour vision only
Why: Sympathetic activity supports rapid responses to challenge.

Q: What does parasympathetic activity generally support?
A) Flight only  B) Rest and digestion*  C) Voluntary sprinting only  D) Bone fracture
Why: Parasympathetic activity supports many resting functions.

Q: Which brain region helps regulate body temperature?
A) Occipital cortex  B) Cerebellar surface  C) Hypothalamus*  D) Corpus callosum
Why: The hypothalamus coordinates several homeostatic responses.

Q: Which brain region is important for forming new episodic memories?
A) Medulla only  B) Retina  C) Pituitary  D) Hippocampus*
Why: The hippocampus supports formation of new episodic memories.

Q: Which brain region is strongly involved in threat processing?
A) Amygdala*  B) Cochlea  C) Thyroid  D) Pons only
Why: The amygdala contributes to threat-related learning and responses.

Q: Which cerebral lobe contains the primary visual cortex?
A) Frontal lobe  B) Occipital lobe*  C) Parietal lobe  D) Insula only
Why: Primary visual processing occurs in the occipital cortex.

Q: Which cerebral lobe contains the primary auditory cortex?
A) Occipital lobe  B) Frontal pole  C) Temporal lobe*  D) Cerebellum
Why: Primary auditory processing occurs in temporal cortex.

Q: Which lobe contains the primary motor cortex?
A) Occipital lobe  B) Temporal pole  C) Cerebellar vermis  D) Frontal lobe*
Why: Primary motor cortex lies in the frontal lobe.

Q: What is cerebrospinal fluid?
A) Fluid within and around the CNS*  B) Bile in the skull  C) Blood without oxygen  D) Joint lubricant
Why: CSF supports and protects CNS structures.

Q: What does neural plasticity mean?
A) Neurons turn into plastic  B) Connections and activity patterns can change*  C) All memories are fixed at birth  D) Every experience destroys all synapses
Why: Plasticity permits adaptation of neural circuits.

Q: What does the blood–brain barrier mainly regulate?
A) Air entering the lungs  B) Food entering the stomach  C) Movement of substances from blood into brain tissue*  D) Tendon movement
Why: The barrier selectively controls exchange with brain tissue.

Why: Blood transports oxygen to tissues.
Source: [https://www.nhlbi.nih.gov/health/heart](https://www.nhlbi.nih.gov/health/heart)

Q: What useful food substances does blood deliver to cells?
A) Nutrients*  B) Pebbles  C) Sunbeams  D) Feathers
Why: Blood distributes many absorbed nutrients.
Source: [https://www.nhlbi.nih.gov/health/heart](https://www.nhlbi.nih.gov/health/heart)

Q: What is the general name for arteries, veins and capillaries?
A) Food pipes  B) Blood vessels*  C) Windpipes  D) Tear ducts
Why: Blood vessels form transport pathways.

Q: What normally happens to your heart during sleep?
A) It turns into bone  B) It disappears  C) It keeps beating*  D) It stops all night
Why: The heart continues supplying blood during sleep.

Q: How does the heart usually respond to active exercise?
A) It always stops  B) It becomes a tooth  C) It moves into the stomach  D) It gets faster*
Why: Working muscles need more blood during activity.

Q: What organ produces the beat you can feel through your chest?
A) Heart*  B) Liver  C) Stomach  D) Kidney
Why: Heart contractions produce the heartbeat.

Q: Which pump moves blood towards the lungs?
A) Brain  B) Heart*  C) Stomach  D) Tongue
Why: The heart pumps blood through the lungs.

Q: What can form over a small damaged blood vessel?
A) A tooth  B) A lens  C) A blood clot*  D) A rib
Why: Clotting helps seal damaged vessels.

Q: Which circulating liquid contains red and white cells?
A) Bile  B) Tears  C) Saliva  D) Blood*
Why: Blood contains several types of cells.

Q: What circulates back to the heart through veins?
A) Blood*  B) Chewed food  C) Air only  D) Urine
Why: Veins return blood towards the heart.

Q: What brings blood into the tissues of the hand?
A) Hair strands  B) Blood vessels*  C) Tooth roots  D) Tear ducts
Why: Blood vessels reach tissues throughout the body.

Q: Which regular body action causes a pulse?
A) Swallowing  B) Blinking  C) Heartbeats*  D) Chewing
Why: Each heartbeat sends a pressure wave through arteries.

Q: Which organ’s main job is circulating blood?
A) Stomach  B) Gall bladder  C) Bladder  D) Heart*
Why: The heart’s contractions move blood.

Q: Why is circulation important for body cells?
A) To deliver oxygen and nutrients*  B) To make sunlight  C) To fill the ears with air  D) To replace every bone
Why: Cells need supplies brought by circulating blood.
Source: [https://www.nhlbi.nih.gov/health/heart](https://www.nhlbi.nih.gov/health/heart)

# Science · Ages 9–11 · Heart and blood

Q: How many chambers does the human heart have?
A) Four*  B) Two  C) Three  D) Six
Why: There are two atria and two ventricles.
Source: [https://www.nhlbi.nih.gov/health/heart/anatomy](https://www.nhlbi.nih.gov/health/heart/anatomy)

Q: What are the heart’s upper chambers called?
A) Ventricles  B) Atria*  C) Bronchi  D) Alveoli
Why: The right and left atria receive returning blood.
Source: [https://www.nhlbi.nih.gov/health/heart/anatomy](https://www.nhlbi.nih.gov/health/heart/anatomy)

Q: What are the lower heart chambers called?
A) Atria  B) Villi  C) Ventricles*  D) Ureters
Why: The ventricles pump blood to lungs and body.
Source: [https://www.nhlbi.nih.gov/health/heart/anatomy](https://www.nhlbi.nih.gov/health/heart/anatomy)

Q: What keeps blood moving the right way through the heart?
A) Taste buds  B) Tendons  C) Alveoli  D) Valves*
Why: Heart valves open and close to guide blood flow.

Q: What carries blood away from the heart?
A) Arteries*  B) Veins  C) Lymph nodes  D) Ureters
Why: Arteries carry blood away from the heart.

Q: What carries blood towards the heart?
A) Arteries  B) Veins*  C) Bronchi  D) Bile ducts
Why: Veins carry blood towards the heart.

Q: What are the smallest exchange blood vessels called?
A) Tendons  B) Bronchi  C) Capillaries*  D) Ligaments
Why: Thin capillary walls allow substances to be exchanged.

Q: Which blood cells mainly transport oxygen?
A) White blood cells  B) Platelets  C) Neurons  D) Red blood cells*
Why: Haemoglobin in red cells carries oxygen.

Q: Which blood cells help fight infection?
A) White blood cells*  B) Red blood cells  C) Cartilage cells  D) Muscle fibres
Why: White cells help defend against pathogens.

Q: Which small blood components help clotting?
A) Neurons  B) Platelets*  C) Alveoli  D) Villi
Why: Platelets help form a plug at damaged vessels.

Q: What is the liquid part of blood called?
A) Bile  B) Mucus  C) Plasma*  D) Synovial fluid
Why: Plasma is the liquid component of blood.

Q: Which gas does blood carry back to the lungs for removal?
A) Helium  B) Neon  C) Argon  D) Carbon dioxide*
Why: Carbon dioxide is produced during cell metabolism.

Q: Which side of the heart pumps blood to the lungs?
A) Right side*  B) Left side  C) Both sides only to the lungs  D) Neither side
Why: The right ventricle sends blood towards the lungs.

Q: Which side pumps blood around the rest of the body?
A) Right side  B) Left side*  C) Only the upper side  D) Neither side
Why: The left ventricle supplies the systemic circulation.

Q: What is the main artery leaving the left ventricle?
A) Vena cava  B) Pulmonary vein  C) Aorta*  D) Ureter
Why: The aorta carries blood into systemic circulation.
Source: [https://www.nhlbi.nih.gov/health/heart/blood-flow](https://www.nhlbi.nih.gov/health/heart/blood-flow)

Q: What is a pulse?
A) An air bubble  B) A nerve cell dividing  C) A stomach contraction  D) A pressure wave caused by a heartbeat*
Why: Heart ejection produces a pressure wave in arteries.

Q: Which vessels return oxygen-rich blood from the lungs?
A) Pulmonary veins*  B) Pulmonary arteries  C) Venae cavae  D) Coronary arteries
Why: Pulmonary veins return oxygenated blood to the heart.

Q: Which artery carries oxygen-poor blood towards the lungs?
A) Aorta  B) Pulmonary artery*  C) Coronary artery  D) Carotid artery
Why: It carries blood from right ventricle to lungs.

Q: What supplies blood to the heart muscle itself?
A) Bile ducts  B) Pulmonary airways  C) Coronary arteries*  D) Ureters
Why: Coronary arteries supply the heart’s own muscle.
Source: [https://www.nhlbi.nih.gov/health/heart/blood-flow](https://www.nhlbi.nih.gov/health/heart/blood-flow)

Q: What separates the right and left sides of the heart?
A) Retina  B) Diaphragm  C) Eardrum  D) Septum*
Why: The septum separates the heart’s right and left sides.
Source: [https://www.nhlbi.nih.gov/health/heart/anatomy](https://www.nhlbi.nih.gov/health/heart/anatomy)

# Science · Ages 12–14 · Heart and blood

Q: How many main blood-filled chambers are in a typical human heart?
A) Two  B) Four*  C) Three  D) Six
Why: There are two atria and two ventricles.

Q: Which chambers receive blood arriving at the heart?

Q: Which structures prevent backward flow within the heart?

Why: Heart valves open and close to guide blood flow.

Q: Which formed blood components contain haemoglobin?

Q: Which cells form part of the body’s immune defence?
A) Red blood cells  B) White blood cells*  C) Cartilage cells  D) Muscle fibres

Q: Which cell fragments gather at damaged blood vessels?
A) Neurons  B) Alveoli  C) Platelets*  D) Villi

Q: In what fluid are blood cells suspended?

A) Left side  B) Right side*  C) Both sides only to the lungs  D) Neither side

Q: Which major artery is an exception to the oxygen-rich-artery rule?

Q: Which vessels deliver oxygen to the myocardium?

# Science · Ages 15–16 · Heart and blood

Q: Which heart chamber has the thickest muscular wall?
A) Left ventricle*  B) Right atrium  C) Left atrium  D) Right ventricle
Why: It must generate pressure for systemic circulation.

Q: What is double circulation?
A) Two hearts working separately  B) Two linked circuits through lungs and body*  C) Blood never returning to the heart  D) Blood flowing only in veins
Why: Pulmonary and systemic circuits are linked through the heart.

Q: Which valve lies between the left atrium and left ventricle?
A) Tricuspid valve  B) Pulmonary valve  C) Mitral valve*  D) Aortic valve
Why: The mitral valve guards the left atrioventricular opening.
Source: [https://www.nhlbi.nih.gov/health/heart/blood-flow](https://www.nhlbi.nih.gov/health/heart/blood-flow)

Q: Which valve lies between the right atrium and right ventricle?
A) Mitral valve  B) Aortic valve  C) Pulmonary valve  D) Tricuspid valve*
Why: The tricuspid valve guards the right atrioventricular opening.
Source: [https://www.nhlbi.nih.gov/health/heart/blood-flow](https://www.nhlbi.nih.gov/health/heart/blood-flow)

Q: Which valve is at the exit from the left ventricle?
A) Aortic valve*  B) Mitral valve  C) Tricuspid valve  D) Pulmonary valve
Why: The aortic valve guards the ventricular outlet to the aorta.
Source: [https://www.nhlbi.nih.gov/health/heart/blood-flow](https://www.nhlbi.nih.gov/health/heart/blood-flow)

Q: What initiates the normal heartbeat?
A) Cerebellum  B) Sinoatrial node*  C) Pituitary gland  D) Gall bladder
Why: The sinoatrial node normally initiates cardiac electrical activity.

Q: What does systole refer to?
A) Filling only  B) Making bile  C) Contracting*  D) Exchanging air
Why: Ventricular systole ejects blood into arteries.

Q: What does diastole refer to?
A) Every valve is permanently open  B) The heart becomes electrically silent forever  C) Blood stops circulating  D) Chambers relax and fill*
Why: Relaxation permits chambers to refill.

Q: What is cardiac output?
A) Blood pumped by one ventricle per minute*  B) Air breathed per second  C) Blood sugar concentration  D) Total blood-cell count
Why: Cardiac output measures flow from a ventricle each minute.

Q: What is stroke volume?
A) Air in one lung  B) Blood pumped per heartbeat*  C) Total plasma in the body  D) Blood remaining in all veins
Why: Stroke volume is the volume ejected per ventricular contraction.

Q: A heart beats 60 times a minute and pumps 70 ml per beat. What is its output?
A) 0.42 litres per minute  B) 42 litres per minute  C) 4.2 litres per minute*  D) 420 litres per minute
Why: 60 × 70 ml = 4,200 ml, or 4.2 litres.

Q: Why are capillary walls very thin?
A) It generates the heartbeat  B) It makes all antibodies  C) It stores bile  D) It gives a short diffusion distance*
Why: Short distances support exchange between blood and tissues.

Q: Why do many veins contain valves?
A) Preventing backward flow*  B) Adding oxygen directly  C) Making red cells  D) Increasing gut digestion
Why: Valves help maintain flow towards the heart.

Q: What is haemoglobin’s main transport role?
A) Digesting starch  B) Binding oxygen reversibly*  C) Filtering urine  D) Emulsifying fat
Why: Haemoglobin binds oxygen in lungs and releases it in tissues.

Q: Why do mature human red blood cells lack a nucleus?
A) Ability to digest bacteria  B) Production of nerve impulses  C) More room for haemoglobin*  D) Greater bone mineral storage
Why: Loss of the nucleus leaves more space for oxygen-carrying haemoglobin.

Q: What does blood plasma mainly consist of?
A) Bone mineral  B) Oxygen gas  C) Fat droplets  D) Water*
Why: Water is the main component of plasma.

Q: Which blood cells can produce antibodies after becoming plasma cells?
A) B lymphocytes*  B) Red blood cells  C) Platelets  D) Osteocytes
Why: Activated B cells can differentiate into plasma cells.

Q: What does a phagocyte do?
A) Turns them into hormones  B) Engulfs and digests them*  C) Carries them to hair  D) Changes them into platelets
Why: Phagocytosis surrounds and breaks down particles or microbes.

Q: Which vessels bring blood from the body to the right atrium?
A) Pulmonary veins  B) Coronary arteries  C) Venae cavae*  D) Carotid arteries
Why: The superior and inferior vena cava enter the right atrium.

Q: What distinguishes an artery from a vein?
A) Blood colour alone  B) Presence of red cells  C) Whether the blood contains water  D) Direction of flow relative to the heart*
Why: Arteries carry blood away; veins carry it towards the heart.

Q: Which chamber has the thickest wall for pumping blood around the body?

Why: It must generate pressure for systemic circulation.

A) Two hearts working separately  B) Blood never returning to the heart  C) Two linked circuits through lungs and body*  D) Blood flowing only in veins
Why: Pulmonary and systemic circuits are linked through the heart.

Why: The mitral valve guards the left atrioventricular opening.

A) Tricuspid valve*  B) Mitral valve  C) Aortic valve  D) Pulmonary valve
Why: The tricuspid valve guards the right atrioventricular opening.

Q: Which valve prevents blood returning from the aorta into the left ventricle?
A) Mitral valve  B) Aortic valve*  C) Tricuspid valve  D) Pulmonary valve
Why: The aortic valve guards the ventricular outlet to the aorta.

Q: Which structure acts as the heart’s usual natural pacemaker?
A) Cerebellum  B) Pituitary gland  C) Sinoatrial node*  D) Gall bladder
Why: The sinoatrial node normally initiates cardiac electrical activity.

Q: During ventricular systole, what are the ventricles doing?
A) Filling only  B) Making bile  C) Exchanging air  D) Contracting*
Why: Ventricular systole ejects blood into arteries.

Q: What happens during the relaxation phase of the cardiac cycle?
A) Chambers relax and fill*  B) Every valve is permanently open  C) The heart becomes electrically silent forever  D) Blood stops circulating
Why: Relaxation permits chambers to refill.

Q: Which quantity equals heart rate multiplied by stroke volume?
A) Air breathed per second  B) Blood pumped by one ventricle per minute*  C) Blood sugar concentration  D) Total blood-cell count
Why: Cardiac output measures flow from a ventricle each minute.

Q: Which volume is ejected by one ventricle during one beat?
A) Air in one lung  B) Total plasma in the body  C) Blood pumped per heartbeat*  D) Blood remaining in all veins
Why: Stroke volume is the volume ejected per ventricular contraction.

Q: What cardiac output results from 60 beats/min and 70 ml/beat?
A) 0.42 litres per minute  B) 42 litres per minute  C) 420 litres per minute  D) 4.2 litres per minute*
Why: 60 × 70 ml = 4,200 ml, or 4.2 litres.

Q: How does a one-cell-thick capillary lining support exchange?
A) It gives a short diffusion distance*  B) It generates the heartbeat  C) It makes all antibodies  D) It stores bile
Why: Short distances support exchange between blood and tissues.

Q: What function is especially useful in veins carrying blood against gravity?
A) Adding oxygen directly  B) Preventing backward flow*  C) Making red cells  D) Increasing gut digestion
Why: Valves help maintain flow towards the heart.

Q: Which molecule allows red cells to carry large quantities of oxygen?
A) Digesting starch  B) Filtering urine  C) Binding oxygen reversibly*  D) Emulsifying fat
Why: Haemoglobin binds oxygen in lungs and releases it in tissues.

Q: What functional advantage comes from the absence of a nucleus in mature red cells?
A) Ability to digest bacteria  B) Production of nerve impulses  C) Greater bone mineral storage  D) More room for haemoglobin*
Why: Loss of the nucleus leaves more space for oxygen-carrying haemoglobin.

Q: Which substance makes up most of plasma?
A) Water*  B) Bone mineral  C) Oxygen gas  D) Fat droplets
Why: Water is the main component of plasma.

Q: Which lymphocytes give rise to antibody-secreting plasma cells?
A) Red blood cells  B) B lymphocytes*  C) Platelets  D) Osteocytes
Why: Activated B cells can differentiate into plasma cells.

Q: How do phagocytic white blood cells attack some pathogens?
A) Turns them into hormones  B) Carries them to hair  C) Engulfs and digests them*  D) Changes them into platelets
Why: Phagocytosis surrounds and breaks down particles or microbes.

Q: Which major veins return systemic blood to the heart?
A) Pulmonary veins  B) Coronary arteries  C) Carotid arteries  D) Venae cavae*
Why: The superior and inferior vena cava enter the right atrium.

Q: Which feature defines these vessel types despite oxygen-level exceptions?
A) Direction of flow relative to the heart*  B) Blood colour alone  C) Presence of red cells  D) Whether the blood contains water
Why: Arteries carry blood away; veins carry it towards the heart.

Q: What is the usual number of lungs in the human chest?
