Why: Humans typically have a right and a left lung.

Q: How does breathing generally change during active exercise?
A) It always stops  B) It gets faster*  C) It turns into chewing  D) It moves to the ears
Why: Exercise increases the body’s need for gas exchange.
Source: [https://www.nhlbi.nih.gov/health/lungs/body-controls-breathing](https://www.nhlbi.nih.gov/health/lungs/body-controls-breathing)

Q: Which action normally continues automatically during sleep?
A) Eating a meal  B) Reading a book  C) Breathing*  D) Tying shoes
Why: Automatic nervous control keeps breathing going.
Source: [https://www.nhlbi.nih.gov/health/lungs/body-controls-breathing](https://www.nhlbi.nih.gov/health/lungs/body-controls-breathing)

Q: What visible change usually accompanies inhalation?
A) Turns into bone  B) Disappears  C) Becomes a tooth  D) Expands*
Why: The chest cavity enlarges during inhalation.

Q: What usually happens to chest size during quiet exhalation?
A) Gets smaller*  B) Keeps expanding forever  C) Turns blue  D) Fills with food
Why: The chest cavity becomes smaller as breathing muscles relax.

Q: Which liquid takes oxygen from lungs to body cells?
A) Saliva  B) Blood*  C) Bile  D) Tears
Why: Blood transports oxygen from the lungs.

Q: Which pump sends blood to the lungs for gas exchange?
A) Stomach  B) Bladder  C) Heart*  D) Tongue
Why: The heart sends blood through lung vessels.

Q: What is another name for the trachea?
A) Food pipe  B) Bile duct  C) Ureter  D) Windpipe*
Why: The windpipe carries air towards the lungs.
Source: [https://www.nhlbi.nih.gov/health/lungs](https://www.nhlbi.nih.gov/health/lungs)

Q: Which protective response forcefully clears air from the airways?
A) Coughing*  B) Chewing  C) Blinking  D) Digesting
Why: Coughing helps clear irritating material.

Q: Which should normally move through the airways?
A) Chewed food  B) Air*  C) Bile  D) Urine
Why: Airways carry air rather than food.

# Science · Ages 9–11 · Breathing

Q: What is the scientific name for the windpipe?
A) Oesophagus  B) Trachea*  C) Aorta  D) Ureter
Why: The trachea conducts air towards the lungs.

Q: What are the two main branches entering the lungs called?
A) Villi  B) Ureters  C) Bronchi*  D) Arteries only
Why: A main bronchus enters each lung.

Q: What are smaller branching airways called?
A) Ventricles  B) Lacteals  C) Tendons  D) Bronchioles*
Why: Bronchioles carry air deeper into the lungs.

Q: What are the tiny lung air sacs called?
A) Alveoli*  B) Villi  C) Neurons  D) Osteons
Why: Alveoli are small sacs with thin walls.
Source: [https://www.nhlbi.nih.gov/health/lungs/breathing-benefits](https://www.nhlbi.nih.gov/health/lungs/breathing-benefits)

Q: Which gas moves from alveoli into blood?
A) Helium  B) Oxygen*  C) Neon  D) Nitrogen only
Why: Oxygen crosses from alveolar air into blood.
Source: [https://www.nhlbi.nih.gov/health/lungs/breathing-benefits](https://www.nhlbi.nih.gov/health/lungs/breathing-benefits)

Q: Which gas moves from blood into alveoli?
A) Hydrogen  B) Argon  C) Carbon dioxide*  D) Helium
Why: Carbon dioxide moves into alveolar air.

Q: What is the main muscle used for breathing?
A) Biceps  B) Triceps  C) Masseter  D) Diaphragm*
Why: The diaphragm is the main breathing muscle.
Source: [https://www.nhlbi.nih.gov/health/lungs/body-controls-breathing](https://www.nhlbi.nih.gov/health/lungs/body-controls-breathing)

Q: What happens to the diaphragm when you breathe in?
A) It contracts and moves down*  B) It contracts and moves up  C) It becomes a bone  D) It closes the nose
Why: Its downward movement increases chest volume.

Q: What happens to the diaphragm during quiet breathing out?
A) It becomes rigid forever  B) It relaxes and moves up*  C) It contracts farther down  D) It enters the stomach
Why: Relaxation reduces the volume of the chest cavity.

Q: What are the muscles between the ribs called?
A) Cardiac valves  B) Abdominal villi  C) Intercostal muscles*  D) Ciliary bones
Why: Intercostal muscles contribute to chest movement.
Source: [https://www.nhlbi.nih.gov/health/lungs/body-controls-breathing](https://www.nhlbi.nih.gov/health/lungs/body-controls-breathing)

Q: What blood vessels surround alveoli?
A) Ureters  B) Bile ducts  C) Lymph nodes  D) Capillaries*
Why: Capillaries bring blood close to alveolar air.

Q: Why do lungs contain many alveoli?
A) A large gas-exchange surface*  B) A smaller oxygen supply  C) A hard bony interior  D) A place to chew food
Why: Numerous alveoli provide a large combined surface.

Q: Why are alveolar walls thin?
A) It prevents all gas movement  B) It gives gases a short distance to cross*  C) It makes bile  D) It stores teeth
Why: A short diffusion distance supports rapid exchange.

Q: Which organ helps control breathing automatically?
A) Stomach  B) Gall bladder  C) Brain*  D) Spleen
Why: Brain centres coordinate breathing muscles.

Q: What happens to oxygen demand during exercise?
A) It always falls to zero  B) It becomes unrelated to movement  C) It changes into nitrogen  D) It rises*
Why: Working muscles use more oxygen in aerobic respiration.

Q: What is gas exchange?
A) Movement of gases across a thin surface*  B) Chewing food  C) Making red cells  D) Filtering urine
Why: Gas exchange swaps gases between air and blood.
Source: [https://www.nhlbi.nih.gov/health/lungs](https://www.nhlbi.nih.gov/health/lungs)

Q: Is breathed-out air completely without oxygen?
A) It contains only carbon dioxide  B) It still contains oxygen*  C) It contains no gases  D) It contains only helium
Why: Only part of inhaled oxygen is taken into the blood.

Q: Which structure helps keep swallowed food out of the airway?
A) Iris  B) Patella  C) Epiglottis*  D) Appendix
Why: The epiglottis helps cover the airway entrance.

Q: What is the voice box called?
A) Pharynx only  B) Rectum  C) Duodenum  D) Larynx*
Why: Vocal folds are located in the larynx.

Q: What do airway mucus and cilia help remove?
A) Trapped particles*  B) New bones  C) Blood cells from marrow  D) Nutrients from villi
Why: Mucus traps particles and cilia move it towards the throat.

# Science · Ages 12–14 · Breathing

Q: Which airway connects the throat region to the bronchi?
A) Oesophagus  B) Aorta  C) Trachea*  D) Ureter
Why: The trachea conducts air towards the lungs.

Q: Into which two main airways does the trachea divide?
A) Villi  B) Ureters  C) Arteries only  D) Bronchi*
Why: A main bronchus enters each lung.

Q: Which small airways lead towards the gas-exchange region?
A) Bronchioles*  B) Ventricles  C) Lacteals  D) Tendons
Why: Bronchioles carry air deeper into the lungs.

Q: Which structures provide the main surface for lung gas exchange?
A) Villi  B) Alveoli*  C) Neurons  D) Osteons
Why: Alveoli are small sacs with thin walls.
Source: [https://www.nhlbi.nih.gov/health/lungs/breathing-benefits](https://www.nhlbi.nih.gov/health/lungs/breathing-benefits)

Q: During normal gas exchange, which gas enters lung capillaries?
A) Helium  B) Neon  C) Oxygen*  D) Nitrogen only
Why: Oxygen crosses from alveolar air into blood.

Q: Which metabolic waste gas enters alveoli for exhalation?
A) Hydrogen  B) Argon  C) Helium  D) Carbon dioxide*
Why: Carbon dioxide moves into alveolar air.

Q: Which dome-shaped muscle lies beneath the lungs?
A) Diaphragm*  B) Biceps  C) Triceps  D) Masseter
Why: The diaphragm is the main breathing muscle.

Q: How does the diaphragm move during inhalation?
A) It contracts and moves up  B) It contracts and moves down*  C) It becomes a bone  D) It closes the nose
Why: Its downward movement increases chest volume.

Q: How does the diaphragm change during normal passive exhalation?
A) It becomes rigid forever  B) It contracts farther down  C) It relaxes and moves up*  D) It enters the stomach
Why: Relaxation reduces the volume of the chest cavity.

Q: Which muscles help move the rib cage during breathing?
A) Cardiac valves  B) Abdominal villi  C) Ciliary bones  D) Intercostal muscles*
Why: Intercostal muscles contribute to chest movement.
Source: [https://www.nhlbi.nih.gov/health/lungs/body-controls-breathing](https://www.nhlbi.nih.gov/health/lungs/body-controls-breathing)

Q: Which tiny vessels are closely associated with alveolar walls?
A) Capillaries*  B) Ureters  C) Bile ducts  D) Lymph nodes
Why: Capillaries bring blood close to alveolar air.

Q: What advantage comes from millions of small air sacs?
A) A smaller oxygen supply  B) A large gas-exchange surface*  C) A hard bony interior  D) A place to chew food
Why: Numerous alveoli provide a large combined surface.

Q: How does a thin alveolar barrier help gas exchange?
A) It prevents all gas movement  B) It makes bile  C) It gives gases a short distance to cross*  D) It stores teeth
Why: A short diffusion distance supports rapid exchange.

Q: Which organ contains centres that regulate breathing rhythm?
A) Stomach  B) Gall bladder  C) Spleen  D) Brain*
Why: Brain centres coordinate breathing muscles.
Source: [https://www.nhlbi.nih.gov/health/lungs/body-controls-breathing](https://www.nhlbi.nih.gov/health/lungs/body-controls-breathing)

Q: How does oxygen demand change when muscles work harder?
A) It rises*  B) It always falls to zero  C) It becomes unrelated to movement  D) It changes into nitrogen
Why: Working muscles use more oxygen in aerobic respiration.

Q: Which process transfers oxygen and carbon dioxide between alveoli and blood?
A) Chewing food  B) Movement of gases across a thin surface*  C) Making red cells  D) Filtering urine
Why: Gas exchange swaps gases between air and blood.
Source: [https://www.nhlbi.nih.gov/health/lungs](https://www.nhlbi.nih.gov/health/lungs)

Q: Which statement about exhaled air is correct?
A) It contains only carbon dioxide  B) It contains no gases  C) It still contains oxygen*  D) It contains only helium
Why: Only part of inhaled oxygen is taken into the blood.

Q: Which flap helps protect the airway during swallowing?
A) Iris  B) Patella  C) Appendix  D) Epiglottis*
Why: The epiglottis helps cover the airway entrance.

Q: Which structure contains the vocal folds?
A) Larynx*  B) Pharynx only  C) Rectum  D) Duodenum
Why: Vocal folds are located in the larynx.

Q: What is moved towards the throat by mucus-lined, ciliated airways?
A) New bones  B) Trapped particles*  C) Blood cells from marrow  D) Nutrients from villi
Why: Mucus traps particles and cilia move it towards the throat.

# Science · Ages 15–16 · Breathing

Q: How does oxygen cross the alveolar barrier?
A) Peristalsis  B) Diffusion*  C) Ossification  D) Filtration into urine
Why: Oxygen diffuses down a partial-pressure gradient.

Q: What happens to pressure in the lungs during inhalation?
A) It becomes infinitely high  B) It equals blood glucose  C) It falls below atmospheric pressure*  D) It stops changing
Why: Air moves from higher atmospheric pressure to lower alveolar pressure.

Q: What happens to the diaphragm during inspiration?
A) It relaxes into a higher dome  B) It turns into cartilage  C) It seals the trachea  D) It contracts and flattens*
Why: Flattening increases the volume of the chest cavity.

Q: Why is quiet expiration usually passive?
A) Elastic recoil after breathing muscles relax*  B) Constant biceps contraction  C) Peristalsis in the oesophagus  D) Active alveolar chewing
Why: Elastic recoil reduces lung volume and raises alveolar pressure.
Source: [https://www.nhlbi.nih.gov/health/lungs/breathing-benefits](https://www.nhlbi.nih.gov/health/lungs/breathing-benefits)

Q: What is ventilation?
A) Oxygen transport in red cells  B) Movement of air into and out of the lungs*  C) Glucose breakdown inside cells  D) Blood production in marrow
Why: Ventilation renews the air available for gas exchange.

Q: Which process releases energy from nutrients inside cells?
A) Air movement only  B) Nasal filtration only  C) Cellular respiration*  D) Vocal-fold vibration
Why: Respiration is cellular energy metabolism; ventilation moves air.

Q: Which molecule carries most oxygen in blood?
A) Bile salts  B) Insulin  C) Amylase  D) Haemoglobin*
Why: Haemoglobin in red cells binds oxygen.
Source: [https://www.nhlbi.nih.gov/health/lungs/breathing-benefits](https://www.nhlbi.nih.gov/health/lungs/breathing-benefits)

Q: What maintains an oxygen gradient at the alveoli?
A) Fresh air and continuous blood circulation*  B) Complete closure of all airways  C) No movement of blood  D) Thickening of the barrier
Why: Air renewal and blood flow maintain gas gradients.

Q: Which feature directly shortens the diffusion pathway?
A) Thick cartilage around each air sac  B) Thin alveolar and capillary walls*  C) Large teeth  D) More abdominal fat
Why: Thin barriers reduce the distance gases must cross.

Q: What is pulmonary surfactant’s main effect?
A) Raises stomach acidity  B) Clots blood  C) Reduces surface tension*  D) Digests protein
Why: Surfactant reduces the tendency of alveoli to collapse.

Q: What is tidal volume?
A) Total blood pumped per beat  B) All air remaining after maximum exhalation  C) Total body water  D) Air inspired or expired per quiet breath*
Why: Tidal volume measures ordinary breath size.

Q: A person takes 12 breaths of 0.5 litres each minute. What is minute ventilation?
A) 6 litres per minute*  B) 0.6 litres per minute  C) 24 litres per minute  D) 60 litres per minute
Why: 12 × 0.5 = 6 litres per minute.

Q: What is residual volume?
A) Air in the stomach  B) Air that cannot be voluntarily exhaled*  C) Blood in the lungs  D) All newly inhaled oxygen
Why: Some air remains in the lungs after maximal expiration.

Q: What is vital capacity?
A) Only one quiet breath  B) All residual air  C) Maximum exhaled volume after breathing in fully*  D) Blood volume in capillaries
Why: Vital capacity excludes residual volume.

Q: What is anatomical dead space?
A) Air in functioning alveoli  B) Blood in pulmonary veins  C) Air dissolved in plasma  D) Air in conducting passages*
Why: Conducting airways move air but are not the main exchange surface.

Q: Which blood change is a major normal stimulus to increased breathing?
A) Rising carbon dioxide*  B) Rising tooth calcium  C) Falling hair pigment  D) Increasing bile storage
Why: CO₂-related changes help regulate breathing.
Source: [https://www.nhlbi.nih.gov/health/lungs/body-controls-breathing](https://www.nhlbi.nih.gov/health/lungs/body-controls-breathing)

Q: Where are important breathing centres located?
A) Retina and iris  B) Medulla and pons*  C) Cerebellum only  D) Pituitary and thyroid
Why: Brainstem networks coordinate rhythmic breathing.

Q: Which lung vessels carry blood towards the heart?
A) Pulmonary arteries  B) Venae cavae  C) Pulmonary veins*  D) Hepatic portal veins
Why: Pulmonary veins carry blood from lungs to heart.

Q: What do cilia do in the conducting airways?
A) Pump blood into alveoli  B) Produce bone  C) Carry oxygen inside red cells  D) Move mucus towards the throat*
Why: Ciliary beating moves particle-laden mucus upwards.

Q: Which statement best describes alveolar gas exchange?
A) Gases diffuse across a thin barrier*  B) Alveoli chew gases  C) Platelets actively carry air through the trachea  D) The diaphragm directly pumps oxygen across cells
Why: Gas movement follows partial-pressure gradients across the barrier.

# Science · Adult · Breathing

Q: What process transfers oxygen from alveolar air into pulmonary blood?

Q: How does alveolar pressure change to draw air into the lungs?
A) It becomes infinitely high  B) It equals blood glucose  C) It stops changing  D) It falls below atmospheric pressure*
Why: Air moves from higher atmospheric pressure to lower alveolar pressure.

Q: Which mechanical change enlarges the thoracic cavity during inhalation?

Why: Flattening increases the volume of the chest cavity.

Q: What normally drives air out during relaxed breathing?

Why: Elastic recoil reduces lung volume and raises alveolar pressure.

Q: Which process moves air between atmosphere and alveoli?
A) Oxygen transport in red cells  B) Glucose breakdown inside cells  C) Movement of air into and out of the lungs*  D) Blood production in marrow
Why: Ventilation renews the air available for gas exchange.

Q: Which process releases energy from nutrients within cells?
A) Air movement only  B) Nasal filtration only  C) Vocal-fold vibration  D) Cellular respiration*
Why: Respiration is cellular energy metabolism; ventilation moves air.

Q: What binds most oxygen after it crosses the alveolar barrier?
A) Haemoglobin*  B) Bile salts  C) Insulin  D) Amylase

Q: Why do ventilation and blood flow together support oxygen diffusion?
A) Complete closure of all airways  B) Fresh air and continuous blood circulation*  C) No movement of blood  D) Thickening of the barrier
Why: Air renewal and blood flow maintain gas gradients.

Q: What structural adaptation reduces distance for alveolar gas transfer?
A) Thick cartilage around each air sac  B) Large teeth  C) Thin alveolar and capillary walls*  D) More abdominal fat

Q: Why does the alveolar lining contain surfactant?
A) Raises stomach acidity  B) Clots blood  C) Digests protein  D) Reduces surface tension*
Why: Surfactant reduces the tendency of alveoli to collapse.

Q: Which volume describes air moved in a normal quiet breath?
A) Air inspired or expired per quiet breath*  B) Total blood pumped per beat  C) All air remaining after maximum exhalation  D) Total body water
Why: Tidal volume measures ordinary breath size.

Q: What minute ventilation results from 12 breaths/min at 0.5 L/breath?
A) 0.6 litres per minute  B) 6 litres per minute*  C) 24 litres per minute  D) 60 litres per minute
Why: 12 × 0.5 = 6 litres per minute.

Q: What air remains after the strongest possible expiration?
A) Air in the stomach  B) Blood in the lungs  C) Air that cannot be voluntarily exhaled*  D) All newly inhaled oxygen
Why: Some air remains in the lungs after maximal expiration.

Q: Which volume can be exhaled after a maximal inhalation?
A) Only one quiet breath  B) All residual air  C) Blood volume in capillaries  D) Maximum exhaled volume after breathing in fully*
Why: Vital capacity excludes residual volume.

Q: Which airway volume does not directly exchange gases with blood?
A) Air in conducting passages*  B) Air in functioning alveoli  C) Blood in pulmonary veins  D) Air dissolved in plasma
Why: Conducting airways move air but are not the main exchange surface.

Q: Under ordinary conditions, which change strongly stimulates respiratory control?
A) Rising tooth calcium  B) Rising carbon dioxide*  C) Falling hair pigment  D) Increasing bile storage
Why: CO₂-related changes help regulate breathing.

Q: Which brainstem regions help regulate the respiratory rhythm?
A) Retina and iris  B) Cerebellum only  C) Medulla and pons*  D) Pituitary and thyroid
Why: Brainstem networks coordinate rhythmic breathing.

Q: Which vessels return oxygenated pulmonary blood to the left atrium?
A) Pulmonary arteries  B) Venae cavae  C) Hepatic portal veins  D) Pulmonary veins*
Why: Pulmonary veins carry blood from lungs to heart.

Q: How does the mucociliary escalator clear inhaled particles?
A) Move mucus towards the throat*  B) Pump blood into alveoli  C) Produce bone  D) Carry oxygen inside red cells
Why: Ciliary beating moves particle-laden mucus upwards.

Q: What distinguishes lung gas exchange from active pumping of gas molecules?
A) Alveoli chew gases  B) Gases diffuse across a thin barrier*  C) Platelets actively carry air through the trachea  D) The diaphragm directly pumps oxygen across cells
Why: Gas movement follows partial-pressure gradients across the barrier.

# Science · Ages 4–5 · Growth and development

Q: What do babies usually do as they get older?
A) Become stones  B) Turn into plants  C) Grow larger*  D) Lose every bone
Why: Children’s bodies grow as they develop.

Q: Which stage comes first in a person’s life?
A) Adulthood  B) Old age  C) The teenage years  D) Babyhood*
Why: Infancy is the earliest stage after birth.

Q: Which usually comes after being a baby?
A) Childhood*  B) Old age  C) Adulthood immediately  D) Retirement
Why: Children develop from infants.

Q: What is a grown-up person called?
A) Infant  B) Adult*  C) Newborn  D) Toddler
Why: Adults have passed through childhood and adolescence.

Q: What helps your body grow?
A) Paint  B) Petrol  C) Food*  D) Smoke
Why: Nutrients provide materials and energy for growth.

Q: What does sleep help children do?
A) Turn into animals  B) Avoid all learning  C) Replace every meal  D) Rest and grow*
Why: Sleep supports development and health.

Q: Where does a baby grow before birth?
A) Womb*  B) Stomach  C) Lung  D) Bladder
Why: The uterus, or womb, supports development before birth.

Q: What joins a growing baby to the placenta?
A) Spinal cord  B) Umbilical cord*  C) Shoe cord  D) Vocal cord
Why: The umbilical cord links the fetus with the placenta.

Q: What grows as a baby’s body gets bigger?
A) Clothes  B) Shoes  C) Bones*  D) Toys
Why: Bones grow with the developing body.

Q: Do all children grow at exactly the same speed?
A) Yes, everyone is identical  B) Only tall children grow  C) Children never grow  D) No, growth rates vary*
Why: Growth differs between individuals.

Q: Which is usually learnt before running?
A) Walking*  B) Driving  C) Writing an essay  D) Riding a motorbike
Why: Walking usually develops before running.

Q: What happens to baby teeth as adult teeth arrive?
A) They become finger bones  B) They fall out*  C) They turn into hair  D) They become lungs
Why: Permanent teeth replace primary teeth.

Q: What can show that your feet have grown?
A) A different eye colour  B) A quieter voice  C) Needing larger shoes*  D) Longer eyelashes only
Why: Growing feet need appropriately larger footwear.

Q: Which life stage usually comes after childhood?
A) Infancy  B) Newborn stage  C) Old age  D) Teenage years*
Why: Adolescence is the transition towards adulthood.

Q: What is learning to do new things called?
A) Development*  B) Digestion  C) Breathing  D) Clotting
Why: Development includes acquiring new skills and abilities.

Q: Which happens as a child learns to hold a pencil?
A) Eye colour  B) Hand control*  C) Blood group  D) Number of lungs
Why: Practice and development improve fine motor control.

Q: What is an older person in the later stage of life called?
A) A newborn  B) A toddler  C) An older adult*  D) An embryo
Why: Older adulthood is a later life stage.

Q: Which stays with you as you grow from a baby?
A) Having exactly the same height  B) Wearing the same shoes  C) Keeping every baby tooth  D) Being the same person*
Why: People grow and change while remaining themselves.

Q: What do growing bodies need to drink?
A) Water*  B) Glue  C) Paint  D) Petrol
Why: Water is necessary for normal body functions.

Q: Which activity helps children practise balance and movement?
A) Never moving  B) Active play*  C) Only watching walls  D) Avoiding every game
Why: Play provides opportunities to develop movement skills.

# Science · Ages 9–11 · Growth and development

Q: What is puberty?
A) A type of digestion  B) A bone injury  C) A period of physical maturation*  D) A blood-clotting step
Why: Puberty involves hormone-driven maturation.

Q: Do people all start puberty at the same age?
A) Yes, everyone starts on one birthday  B) Only adults experience it  C) It happens before birth  D) No, normal timing varies*
Why: Puberty starts at different times in different people.

Q: What is a growth spurt?
A) A period of faster growth*  B) A sudden loss of every bone  C) A type of sleep  D) A blood group
Why: Growth can accelerate during puberty.

Q: Which body substances help control puberty?
A) Tooth enamel  B) Hormones*  C) Bile salts only  D) Earwax
Why: Hormones coordinate many developmental changes.

Q: What is fertilisation?
A) Food entering the stomach  B) A bone breaking  C) Union of sperm and egg*  D) Air entering the lungs
Why: Fertilisation begins the development of a new organism.

Q: What is the fertilised egg called?
A) Neuron  B) Platelet  C) Alveolus  D) Zygote*
Why: A zygote is the fertilised egg cell.

Q: Where does a fetus usually develop?
A) Uterus*  B) Stomach  C) Lung  D) Kidney
Why: The uterus is the womb.

Q: What is the placenta?
A) A chamber of the heart  B) An organ supporting exchange during pregnancy*  C) A bone in the ear  D) A part of the eye
Why: The placenta exchanges nutrients, gases and wastes.

Q: What does the umbilical cord connect?
A) Stomach and lung  B) Brain and ear  C) Fetus and placenta*  D) Kidney and bladder
Why: Umbilical vessels link the fetus with the placenta.

Q: What is amniotic fluid?
A) Blood in the heart  B) Bile in the liver  C) Urine in the bladder only  D) Fluid in the amniotic sac*
Why: Amniotic fluid surrounds and cushions the fetus.

Q: How many chromosome pairs are usually in a human body cell?
A) 23*  B) 12  C) 24  D) 46
Why: Typical body cells contain 46 chromosomes in 23 pairs.
Source: [https://www.genome.gov/genetics-glossary](https://www.genome.gov/genetics-glossary)

Q: What do genes contain?
A) Tiny pieces of food  B) Instructions encoded in DNA*  C) Air bubbles  D) Bone fragments
Why: Genes carry inherited biological information.
Source: [https://www.genome.gov/genetics-glossary](https://www.genome.gov/genetics-glossary)

Q: Where do children get inherited genetic information?
A) Only teachers  B) Only friends  C) Both biological parents*  D) Only grandparents directly
Why: A child normally receives a chromosome set from each biological parent.
Source: [https://www.genome.gov/genetics-glossary](https://www.genome.gov/genetics-glossary)

Q: What is cell division?
A) A tooth dissolving  B) A lung taking air  C) A heart valve closing  D) A cell producing daughter cells*
Why: Cell division increases or renews cell populations.

Q: How do cells help the body grow?
A) They increase in number and can grow larger*  B) They all turn into fat  C) They stop using energy  D) They disappear permanently
Why: Growth involves changes in cell number and size.

Q: What are identical twins formed from?
A) Two unrelated adult cells  B) One fertilised egg that splits*  C) Two stomachs  D) One unfertilised egg dividing alone
Why: A single early embryo separates into two developing embryos.

Q: What are non-identical twins usually formed from?
A) One red cell dividing  B) One bone splitting  C) Two eggs fertilised by two sperm*  D) Two unfertilised eggs only
Why: Two separate fertilisations produce two embryos.

Q: What is adolescence?
A) Only the first month after birth  B) Only old age  C) The time before fertilisation  D) The period between childhood and adulthood*
Why: Adolescence includes physical and social development.

Q: What is fine motor development?
A) Improving control of small muscles*  B) Only increasing height  C) Changing blood group  D) Making new ribs
Why: Fine motor skills use controlled small movements.

# Science · Ages 15–16 · Growth and development

Q: What type of cell division usually supports body growth?
A) Meiosis  B) Fertilisation  C) Mitosis*  D) Diffusion
Why: Mitosis preserves chromosome number in typical daughter cells.
Source: [https://www.genome.gov/genetics-glossary/Mitosis](https://www.genome.gov/genetics-glossary/Mitosis)

Q: What type of cell division produces gametes?
A) Mitosis only  B) Peristalsis  C) Ossification  D) Meiosis*
Why: Meiosis produces haploid cells from diploid precursors.
Source: [https://www.genome.gov/genetics-glossary/Meiosis](https://www.genome.gov/genetics-glossary/Meiosis)

Q: How many chromosomes are usually in a human gamete?
A) 23*  B) 46  C) 92  D) 12
Why: Gametes usually contain one chromosome set.
Source: [https://www.genome.gov/genetics-glossary/Meiosis](https://www.genome.gov/genetics-glossary/Meiosis)

Q: What chromosome number is restored by normal human fertilisation?
A) 23  B) 46*  C) 69  D) 92
Why: 23 chromosomes from each gamete restore the diploid number.
Source: [https://www.genome.gov/genetics-glossary/Meiosis](https://www.genome.gov/genetics-glossary/Meiosis)

Q: What is implantation?
A) Release of an egg  B) Formation of sperm  C) Attachment and embedding in the endometrium*  D) Loss of a tooth
Why: Implantation establishes the embryo within the uterine lining.

Q: What is ovulation?
A) Implantation  B) Menstruation  C) Fertilisation  D) Release of an oocyte*
Why: Ovulation releases an oocyte from an ovarian follicle.

Q: Where does human fertilisation usually occur?
A) Fallopian tube*  B) Stomach  C) Cervix  D) Urinary bladder
Why: Fertilisation most often occurs in a uterine tube.

Q: What is the endometrium?
A) The outer skin  B) The inner uterine lining*  C) The heart lining  D) The lung surface
Why: The endometrium prepares for possible implantation.

Q: What is menstruation?
A) The whole ovary  B) The whole uterus  C) Part of the uterine lining with blood*  D) The entire placenta every month
Why: Hormonal changes cause shedding of the endometrium.

Q: What is differentiation?
A) Loss of all DNA  B) Digestion of every protein  C) Conversion of cells into air  D) Development of specialised cell types*
Why: Differentiation produces specialised cells through altered gene expression.

Q: What is a stem cell?
A) A cell with self-renewal and differentiation capacity*  B) Any mature red blood cell  C) A bone mineral  D) A hormone receptor
Why: Stem cells can divide and give rise to differentiated cells.

Q: What does genotype describe?
A) Visible traits only  B) Genetic makeup*  C) Age alone  D) Daily food intake
Why: Genotype refers to genetic information carried by an individual.
Source: [https://www.genome.gov/genetics-glossary](https://www.genome.gov/genetics-glossary)

Q: What does phenotype describe?
A) Only the DNA sequence  B) Only the number of chromosomes  C) Expressed characteristics*  D) Only biological age
Why: Phenotype reflects genetic and environmental influences.
Source: [https://www.genome.gov/genetics-glossary](https://www.genome.gov/genetics-glossary)

Q: How can nutrition affect growth?
A) Food replaces chromosomes  B) Every nutrient changes blood group  C) Nutrition has no biological effects  D) Environment also influences development*
Why: Growth depends on inherited potential and environmental conditions.

Q: What is the main exchange function of the placenta?
A) Gases, nutrients and wastes*  B) Whole bones  C) Chewed food pieces  D) Air through an umbilical airway
Why: Placental exchange supports fetal metabolism.

Q: Do maternal and fetal blood normally mix directly in the placenta?
A) They form one shared heart  B) They remain in separate circulations across an exchange barrier*  C) Fetal blood contains no cells  D) Maternal blood flows directly through fetal lungs
Why: Exchange occurs across placental tissues between distinct circulations.

Q: What is genetic variation?
A) A change only in clothing  B) A universal identical genome  C) Differences in genetic makeup*  D) A type of breathing
Why: Genetic variation contributes to differences between individuals.
Source: [https://www.genome.gov/genetics-glossary](https://www.genome.gov/genetics-glossary)

Q: Why can non-identical siblings differ genetically?
A) Their parents have no genes  B) All siblings share identical gametes  C) Genes appear only after birth  D) Gametes carry different combinations of alleles*
Why: Meiosis and fertilisation create different allele combinations.

Q: What is senescence?
A) Age-related biological decline or cell ageing*  B) Fertilisation  C) Embryo implantation  D) Pubertal growth alone
Why: Senescence describes aspects of biological ageing.

Q: What is menopause?
A) The start of puberty  B) Permanent end of menstruation*  C) A single missed period  D) Release of the first egg
Why: Menopause marks the end of reproductive menstrual cycling.

Q: What chromosome number is typical of a mature human sperm or egg?
A) 46  B) 23*  C) 92  D) 12
Why: Gametes usually contain one chromosome set.

Q: When two typical human gametes unite, how many chromosomes result?
A) 23  B) 69  C) 46*  D) 92
Why: 23 chromosomes from each gamete restore the diploid number.
Source: [https://www.genome.gov/genetics-glossary/Meiosis](https://www.genome.gov/genetics-glossary/Meiosis)

Q: What occurs when an early embryo embeds in the uterine lining?
A) Release of an egg  B) Formation of sperm  C) Loss of a tooth  D) Attachment and embedding in the endometrium*
Why: Implantation establishes the embryo within the uterine lining.

Q: Which event releases an egg from an ovary?
A) Release of an oocyte*  B) Implantation  C) Menstruation  D) Fertilisation
Why: Ovulation releases an oocyte from an ovarian follicle.

Q: In a typical natural conception, where do sperm and egg usually unite?
A) Stomach  B) Fallopian tube*  C) Cervix  D) Urinary bladder
Why: Fertilisation most often occurs in a uterine tube.

Q: Which uterine tissue changes across the menstrual cycle?
A) The outer skin  B) The heart lining  C) The inner uterine lining*  D) The lung surface
Why: The endometrium prepares for possible implantation.

Q: What is shed when pregnancy does not occur in a typical menstrual cycle?
A) The whole ovary  B) The whole uterus  C) The entire placenta every month  D) Part of the uterine lining with blood*
Why: Hormonal changes cause shedding of the endometrium.

Q: How do unspecialised cells acquire distinct structures and functions?
A) Development of specialised cell types*  B) Loss of all DNA  C) Digestion of every protein  D) Conversion of cells into air
Why: Differentiation produces specialised cells through altered gene expression.

Q: Which cell type can self-renew and generate more specialised cells?
A) Any mature red blood cell  B) A cell with self-renewal and differentiation capacity*  C) A bone mineral  D) A hormone receptor
Why: Stem cells can divide and give rise to differentiated cells.

Q: Which term refers to an organism’s genetic constitution?
A) Visible traits only  B) Age alone  C) Genetic makeup*  D) Daily food intake
Why: Genotype refers to genetic information carried by an individual.
Source: [https://www.genome.gov/genetics-glossary](https://www.genome.gov/genetics-glossary)

Q: Which term includes observable characteristics influenced by genes and environment?
A) Only the DNA sequence  B) Only the number of chromosomes  C) Only biological age  D) Expressed characteristics*
Why: Phenotype reflects genetic and environmental influences.

Q: Why is growth not determined by genes alone?
A) Environment also influences development*  B) Food replaces chromosomes  C) Every nutrient changes blood group  D) Nutrition has no biological effects
Why: Growth depends on inherited potential and environmental conditions.

Q: Which substances normally pass between maternal and fetal systems at the placenta?
A) Whole bones  B) Gases, nutrients and wastes*  C) Chewed food pieces  D) Air through an umbilical airway
Why: Placental exchange supports fetal metabolism.

Q: Which description of normal placental circulation is correct?
A) They form one shared heart  B) Fetal blood contains no cells  C) They remain in separate circulations across an exchange barrier*  D) Maternal blood flows directly through fetal lungs
Why: Exchange occurs across placental tissues between distinct circulations.

Q: What term describes differences in inherited genetic information among individuals?
A) A change only in clothing  B) A universal identical genome  C) A type of breathing  D) Differences in genetic makeup*
Why: Genetic variation contributes to differences between individuals.

Q: Why are siblings from the same parents usually not genetically identical?
A) Gametes carry different combinations of alleles*  B) Their parents have no genes  C) All siblings share identical gametes  D) Genes appear only after birth
Why: Meiosis and fertilisation create different allele combinations.

Q: Which term refers to biological changes associated with ageing?
A) Fertilisation  B) Age-related biological decline or cell ageing*  C) Embryo implantation  D) Pubertal growth alone
Why: Senescence describes aspects of biological ageing.

Q: Which event marks the end of menstrual cycles due to loss of ovarian follicular activity?
A) The start of puberty  B) A single missed period  C) Permanent end of menstruation*  D) Release of the first egg
Why: Menopause marks the end of reproductive menstrual cycling.

Why: Hormones help regulate growth.

Q: Can body messages help your body use food?

Q: What do we call body parts that make hormones?

Q: Which belongs inside your body?
A) A hormone*  B) A pencil  C) A shoe  D) A spoon
Why: Hormones are substances produced within the body.

A) They are tiny teeth  B) They help body parts communicate*  C) They are swallowed toys  D) They are bones in the ear
Why: Hormones signal to responsive cells.

Why: Body control systems help regulate thirst.

Why: Endocrine hormones travel within the body.

A) Only during maths  B) Only when you clap  C) No  D) Yes*
Why: Hormonal control usually occurs automatically.

Q: Which body messenger helps control sugar in your blood?

Why: Insulin helps control blood glucose.

Q: Does your body have more than one kind of hormone?
A) There is only one  B) There are many kinds*  C) Hormones exist only in teeth  D) They are all bones

Q: Can body messages help the body work together?

# Science · Ages 9–11 · Hormones

Q: What enables a particular cell to respond to a hormone?

Q: Which organ makes insulin?

Why: Insulin is made by pancreatic beta cells.

Q: What does insulin help control?
A) Glucose level*  B) Hair length only  C) Pupil colour  D) Number of ribs
Why: Insulin helps lower elevated blood glucose.

Q: Which hormone prepares the body for fight or flight?
A) Melatonin  B) Adrenaline*  C) Calcitonin  D) Prolactin

Q: Where are the adrenal glands?
A) Inside the eyes  B) Inside the teeth  C) Above the kidneys*  D) Below the kneecaps

Q: Where is the thyroid gland?
A) Inside the ankle  B) In the palm  C) Behind the knee  D) Front of the neck*

Q: What do thyroid hormones help control?
A) Metabolic rate*  B) Only eye colour  C) Only tooth number  D) Only hearing pitch
Why: Thyroid hormones help regulate energy use.

Q: Which small gland at the brain’s base releases growth hormone?
A) Gall bladder  B) Pituitary*  C) Spleen  D) Salivary gland
Why: The anterior pituitary secretes growth hormone.

Q: What does growth hormone support?
A) Making sunlight  B) Air entering the nose  C) Growth of body tissues*  D) Changing blood group
Why: Growth hormone supports tissue growth and metabolism.

Q: Which hormone helps signal night-time?
A) Insulin  B) Adrenaline  C) Glucagon  D) Melatonin*
Why: Melatonin helps signal the body’s biological night.

Q: Which gland makes melatonin?
A) Pineal gland*  B) Thyroid  C) Adrenal cortex  D) Pancreas
Why: The pineal gland releases melatonin.

Q: Which brain region links nervous and hormonal control?
A) Retina  B) Hypothalamus*  C) Cochlea  D) Cerebellar cortex
Why: The hypothalamus links neural information with endocrine responses.

Q: Which hormone raises blood glucose when needed?
A) Melatonin  B) Oxytocin  C) Glucagon*  D) Calcitonin
Why: Glucagon promotes an increase in blood glucose.

Q: Which organs produce eggs and several reproductive hormones?
A) Lungs  B) Kidneys  C) Tear glands  D) Ovaries*
Why: Ovaries produce oocytes and reproductive hormones.

Q: Which organs produce sperm and testosterone?
A) Testes*  B) Thyroid  C) Pancreas  D) Salivary glands
Why: The testes produce sperm and androgens.

Q: Are hormones involved in puberty?
A) No, only bones act  B) Yes, hormones are involved*  C) Only air controls puberty  D) Only teeth control it
Why: Puberty depends on changing hormone signals.

Q: What happens when hormone output is adjusted to the body’s needs?
A) It removes every receptor  B) It stops all growth  C) It helps maintain balance*  D) It changes all blood to water
Why: Feedback helps keep internal conditions within suitable ranges.

# Science · Ages 15–16 · Hormones

Q: What is negative feedback?
A) It always accelerates production  B) It destroys every receptor  C) It converts hormones into bones  D) It reduces further production*
Why: Negative feedback limits deviation from a regulated state.

Q: Which pancreatic cells secrete insulin?
A) Beta cells*  B) Alpha cells  C) Red blood cells  D) Osteoclasts
Why: Pancreatic beta cells secrete insulin.
Source: [https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK613062/](https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK613062/)

Q: Which pancreatic cells secrete glucagon?
A) Beta cells  B) Alpha cells*  C) Platelets  D) Oligodendrocytes
Why: Pancreatic alpha cells secrete glucagon.
Source: [https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK613062/](https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK613062/)

Q: How does insulin lower blood glucose?
A) Preventing all glucose uptake  B) Breaking every red cell  C) Promoting glucose uptake and storage*  D) Stopping all liver function
Why: Insulin supports glucose uptake and storage in responsive tissues.
Source: [https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK613062/](https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK613062/)

Q: How does glucagon help raise blood glucose?
A) Removal of every liver receptor  B) Permanent closure of bile ducts  C) Conversion of glucose into oxygen  D) Release and production of glucose*
Why: Glucagon promotes hepatic glucose output.
Source: [https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK613062/](https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK613062/)

Q: What is ADH’s main water-balance effect?
A) Increases water reabsorption*  B) Stops all filtration permanently  C) Adds glucose to every nephron  D) Makes bile
Why: ADH helps conserve body water.

Q: Where is ADH synthesised?
A) Cerebellum  B) Hypothalamus*  C) Pineal gland  D) Thyroid
Why: Hypothalamic neurons synthesise ADH.

Q: Which gland releases ADH into circulation?
A) Anterior pituitary  B) Thyroid  C) Posterior pituitary*  D) Pancreatic islets
Why: The posterior pituitary releases hypothalamic ADH.

Q: Which hormone stimulates the thyroid gland?
A) ADH  B) Insulin  C) Melatonin  D) TSH*
Why: Thyroid-stimulating hormone acts on the thyroid.

Q: Which hormone stimulates the adrenal cortex to release cortisol?
A) ACTH*  B) FSH  C) Insulin  D) Calcitonin
Why: ACTH stimulates cortisol secretion by the adrenal cortex.

Q: Which adrenal region secretes adrenaline?
A) Adrenal cortex  B) Adrenal medulla*  C) Renal cortex  D) Thyroid follicle
Why: The adrenal medulla secretes catecholamines.

Q: Which adrenal region secretes cortisol?
A) Adrenal medulla  B) Pineal gland  C) Adrenal cortex*  D) Posterior pituitary
Why: The adrenal cortex produces cortisol.

Q: What is cortisol?
A) A digestive enzyme  B) A blood-cell fragment  C) A bone mineral  D) An adrenal steroid hormone*
Why: Cortisol influences metabolism and stress adaptation.

Q: What is the main effect of aldosterone in the kidney?
A) Promotes sodium reabsorption*  B) Removes every sodium ion  C) Produces red cells directly  D) Stops all urine formation
Why: Aldosterone supports sodium retention and potassium excretion.

Q: Which hormone increases blood calcium when it is low?
A) Insulin  B) Parathyroid hormone*  C) Melatonin  D) ADH
Why: PTH acts to increase circulating calcium.

Q: Which hormone supports uterine contractions during labour?
A) Glucagon  B) Thyroxine  C) Oxytocin*  D) Calcitonin
Why: Oxytocin can intensify uterine contractions.

Q: Which hormone chiefly supports milk production after birth?
A) ADH  B) Glucagon  C) Aldosterone  D) Prolactin*
Why: Prolactin promotes mammary milk production.

Q: Which hormone triggers milk ejection?
A) Oxytocin*  B) Insulin  C) Cortisol only  D) Thyroxine
Why: Oxytocin causes the milk-ejection reflex.

Q: What distinguishes endocrine from exocrine secretion?
A) Both always use ducts  B) Endocrine signals enter blood; exocrine products use ducts*  C) Endocrine glands produce only saliva  D) Exocrine glands release only blood cells
Why: Endocrine communication does not use a duct to its target.

Q: Why can hormones act on distant organs?
A) Hormones move only through bones  B) Target cells need no receptors  C) Circulation carries hormones to receptor-bearing cells*  D) Every hormone remains in its gland
Why: Blood transport connects glands with distant target tissues.
Source: [https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/sites/books/NBK22231/](https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/sites/books/NBK22231/)

Why: Insulin supports glucose uptake and storage in responsive tissues.

A) Release and production of glucose*  B) Removal of every liver receptor  C) Permanent closure of bile ducts  D) Conversion of glucose into oxygen

A) Stops all filtration permanently  B) Increases water reabsorption*  C) Adds glucose to every nephron  D) Makes bile

Q: Which brain region produces ADH before its posterior-pituitary release?

A) Anterior pituitary  B) Thyroid  C) Pancreatic islets  D) Posterior pituitary*

Q: Which pituitary hormone is central to the cortisol response?

Why: ACTH stimulates cortisol secretion by the adrenal cortex.

Q: Which part of the adrenal gland releases epinephrine?
A) Adrenal cortex  B) Renal cortex  C) Adrenal medulla*  D) Thyroid follicle
Why: The adrenal medulla secretes catecholamines.

Q: Which part of the adrenal gland produces glucocorticoids?
A) Adrenal medulla  B) Pineal gland  C) Posterior pituitary  D) Adrenal cortex*
Why: The adrenal cortex produces cortisol.

Q: Which hormone is a glucocorticoid involved in metabolic stress responses?
A) An adrenal steroid hormone*  B) A digestive enzyme  C) A blood-cell fragment  D) A bone mineral
Why: Cortisol influences metabolism and stress adaptation.

Q: How does aldosterone contribute to salt balance?
A) Removes every sodium ion  B) Promotes sodium reabsorption*  C) Produces red cells directly  D) Stops all urine formation
Why: Aldosterone supports sodium retention and potassium excretion.

Q: Which parathyroid hormone helps restore low plasma calcium?
A) Insulin  B) Melatonin  C) Parathyroid hormone*  D) ADH
Why: PTH acts to increase circulating calcium.

Q: Which hormone participates in positive feedback during childbirth?
A) Glucagon  B) Thyroxine  C) Calcitonin  D) Oxytocin*
Why: Oxytocin can intensify uterine contractions.

Q: Which anterior-pituitary hormone promotes milk synthesis?
A) Prolactin*  B) ADH  C) Glucagon  D) Aldosterone
Why: Prolactin promotes mammary milk production.

Q: Which hormone contracts cells around mammary glands to release milk?
A) Insulin  B) Oxytocin*  C) Cortisol only  D) Thyroxine
Why: Oxytocin causes the milk-ejection reflex.

Q: Which comparison between endocrine and exocrine glands is correct?
A) Both always use ducts  B) Endocrine glands produce only saliva  C) Endocrine signals enter blood; exocrine products use ducts*  D) Exocrine glands release only blood cells
Why: Endocrine communication does not use a duct to its target.

Q: What makes long-distance endocrine communication possible?
A) Hormones move only through bones  B) Target cells need no receptors  C) Every hormone remains in its gland  D) Circulation carries hormones to receptor-bearing cells*
Why: Blood transport connects glands with distant target tissues.

A) Change the weather  B) Learn about body parts*  C) Grow extra fingers  D) Replace every doctor

A) William Harvey  B) Robert Hooke*  C) Joseph Lister  D) René Laennec

Q: Which instrument helped Antonie van Leeuwenhoek study microbes?
A) Stethoscope  B) Barometer  C) Microscope*  D) Compass
Why: Microscopes revealed structures invisible to the unaided eye.

Q: Who is associated with the discovery of X-rays?
A) Edward Jenner  B) William Harvey  C) Robert Hooke  D) Wilhelm Röntgen*
Why: Röntgen discovered a penetrating form of radiation.
Source: [https://collection.sciencemuseumgroup.org.uk/objects/co134691](https://collection.sciencemuseumgroup.org.uk/objects/co134691)

Q: Who developed an influential early smallpox vaccine?
A) Edward Jenner*  B) Alexander Fleming  C) Joseph Lister  D) Robert Hooke
Why: Jenner investigated cowpox-based protection against smallpox.
Source: [https://collection.sciencemuseumgroup.org.uk/people/cp37470/edward-jenner](https://collection.sciencemuseumgroup.org.uk/people/cp37470/edward-jenner)

Q: Who discovered penicillin’s antibacterial effect?
A) William Harvey  B) Alexander Fleming*  C) Edward Jenner  D) Andreas Vesalius
Why: Fleming observed the antibacterial action associated with penicillin.

Q: Who is closely associated with antiseptic surgery?
A) Robert Hooke  B) René Laennec  C) Joseph Lister*  D) William Harvey
Why: Lister developed an influential antiseptic surgical system.
Source: [https://collection.sciencemuseumgroup.org.uk/people/cp37522/joseph-lister](https://collection.sciencemuseumgroup.org.uk/people/cp37522/joseph-lister)

Q: What does an anaesthetic help control during an operation?
A) Eye colour  B) Blood group  C) Number of chromosomes  D) Pain and sensation*
Why: Anaesthesia permits procedures with reduced or absent sensation.

Q: What does an antiseptic help reduce?
A) Microorganisms that can cause infection*  B) All bone tissue  C) All oxygen in the blood  D) Every hormone
Why: Antiseptics reduce or inhibit microorganisms on living tissue.

Q: What does germ theory explain?
A) All illness is caused by weather  B) Microbes can cause disease*  C) Every illness has one cause  D) Germs are tiny bones
Why: Germ theory connected microorganisms with particular diseases.

Q: Which ancient physician is linked with a famous medical oath?
A) Röntgen  B) Fleming  C) Hippocrates*  D) Banting
Why: The oath belongs to the Hippocratic medical tradition.

Q: Who wrote an influential Renaissance anatomy book in 1543?
A) Edward Jenner  B) Alexander Fleming  C) René Laennec  D) Andreas Vesalius*
Why: Vesalius used direct anatomical study to improve body descriptions.
Source: [https://www.rcseng.ac.uk/-/media/files/rcs/museums-and-shop/archives/human-dissection-factsheet.pdf](https://www.rcseng.ac.uk/-/media/files/rcs/museums-and-shop/archives/human-dissection-factsheet.pdf)

Q: What does dissection mean?
A) Examining a body’s internal parts by cutting*  B) Listening through a stethoscope  C) Measuring temperature  D) Photographing the skin only
Why: Dissection reveals internal anatomical relationships.

Q: What does anatomy study?
A) Only the weather  B) Body structure*  C) Only medicines’ prices  D) Only stars
Why: Anatomy concerns the arrangement of body parts.

Q: What does physiology study?
A) Only bone names  B) Only old books  C) Body function*  D) Only hospital buildings
Why: Physiology examines how living systems function.

Q: What is an endoscope used for?
A) Measuring shoe size  B) Making hormones  C) Counting external hairs only  D) Viewing inside the body*
Why: Endoscopes allow internal examination through openings or small incisions.

Q: What does ultrasound use to make images?
A) High-frequency sound*  B) Visible light only  C) X-rays  D) Radioactive particles
Why: Ultrasound forms images from sound echoes.

Q: What does MRI use to help form images?
A) Only visible light  B) Magnetic fields and radio waves*  C) Only sound echoes  D) Only ordinary photographs
Why: MRI uses magnetic fields and radio-frequency signals.

Q: Why did scientists compare observations with old anatomy books?
A) It made evidence unnecessary  B) It stopped all research  C) It helped reveal errors and test descriptions*  D) It proved every old claim correct
Why: Observed structures can challenge inherited descriptions.
Source: [https://www.rcseng.ac.uk/-/media/files/rcs/museums-and-shop/archives/human-dissection-factsheet.pdf](https://www.rcseng.ac.uk/-/media/files/rcs/museums-and-shop/archives/human-dissection-factsheet.pdf)

Q: Why should discoveries be recorded and shared?
A) It prevents every disagreement  B) It replaces all testing  C) It makes all ideas true  D) Others can check and build on the work*
Why: Sharing methods and results supports scrutiny and further study.

# Science · Ages 15–16 · Medical history

Q: In which year did Harvey publish De motu cordis?
A) 1628*  B) 1543  C) 1665  D) 1895
Why: Harvey published his account of circulation in 1628.
Source: [https://www.rcplondon.ac.uk/media/pwbhu50c/rcp-harveian-oration-2015.pdf](https://www.rcplondon.ac.uk/media/pwbhu50c/rcp-harveian-oration-2015.pdf)

Q: In which year was Hooke’s Micrographia published?
A) 1628  B) 1665*  C) 1796  D) 1928
Why: Micrographia appeared in 1665.
Source: [https://wellcomecollection.org/works/apmaw56u](https://wellcomecollection.org/works/apmaw56u)

Q: In which year did Jenner perform his famous cowpox inoculation?
A) 1665  B) 1816  C) 1796*  D) 1895
Why: Jenner performed the experiment in 1796.
Source: [https://collection.sciencemuseumgroup.org.uk/people/cp37470/edward-jenner](https://collection.sciencemuseumgroup.org.uk/people/cp37470/edward-jenner)

Q: What substance did Lister use as an antiseptic?
A) Insulin  B) Glucose  C) Melatonin  D) Carbolic acid*
Why: Carbolic acid is also called phenol.
Source: [https://collection.sciencemuseumgroup.org.uk/people/cp37522/joseph-lister](https://collection.sciencemuseumgroup.org.uk/people/cp37522/joseph-lister)

Q: Which discovery let doctors image bones without dissection?
A) X-rays*  B) The stethoscope  C) The microscope alone  D) The thermometer
Why: X-rays enabled internal imaging through the body.
Source: [https://collection.sciencemuseumgroup.org.uk/objects/co134691](https://collection.sciencemuseumgroup.org.uk/objects/co134691)

Q: What was the main limitation of relying only on ancient texts?
A) Every old text was accurate  B) Descriptions could contain untested errors*  C) Observation was impossible  D) Anatomy never varies
Why: Direct evidence can reveal inaccuracies in authoritative accounts.

Q: Why was Harvey’s quantitative reasoning important?
A) It proved blood had no cells  B) It showed the lungs made all blood  C) The volume was too large for continual replacement by food*  D) It made observation unnecessary
Why: Repeated pumping implied that blood must recirculate.

Q: Which scientist helped identify the link between pancreas and fat digestion?
A) Edward Jenner  B) Wilhelm Röntgen  C) René Laennec  D) Claude Bernard*
Why: Bernard investigated pancreatic digestive functions.

Q: Which two researchers shared the 1923 medicine Nobel for insulin?
A) Frederick Banting and John Macleod*  B) Robert Hooke and William Harvey  C) Edward Jenner and Joseph Lister  D) Watson and Crick
Why: Banting and Macleod were the named 1923 laureates.
Source: [https://www.nobelprize.org/prizes/medicine/1923/banting/lecture/](https://www.nobelprize.org/prizes/medicine/1923/banting/lecture/)

Q: Why is crediting only one person for insulin’s development misleading?
A) No experiments were performed  B) Several researchers made important contributions*  C) Insulin was discovered in ancient Egypt  D) One person did all work without help
Why: Banting, Best, Macleod and Collip all contributed.
Source: [https://www.diabetes.org.uk/our-research/about-our-research/our-impact/discovery-of-insulin?trk=article-ssr-frontend-pulse_little-text-block](https://www.diabetes.org.uk/our-research/about-our-research/our-impact/discovery-of-insulin?trk=article-ssr-frontend-pulse_little-text-block)

Q: Which three researchers shared the 1945 medicine Nobel for penicillin?
A) Harvey, Hooke and Jenner  B) Banting, Best and Macleod  C) Fleming, Chain and Florey*  D) Röntgen, Lister and Laennec
Why: The prize recognised Fleming, Chain and Florey.
Source: [https://www.phc.ox.ac.uk/blog/penicillin-in-oxford-four-plaques-and-a-memorial](https://www.phc.ox.ac.uk/blog/penicillin-in-oxford-four-plaques-and-a-memorial)

Q: Why did penicillin require more than its initial discovery?
A) Proof that mould had bones  B) Elimination of all clinical testing  C) Replacement of every vaccine  D) Development into a usable, producible treatment*
Why: Purification, testing and production made therapeutic use possible.

Q: Which pair shared the 1906 medicine Nobel for nervous-system structure?
A) Camillo Golgi and Santiago Ramón y Cajal*  B) Harvey and Hooke  C) Jenner and Lister  D) Banting and Macleod
Why: Golgi and Cajal were recognised for nervous-system research.
Source: [https://www.nobelprize.org/prizes/medicine/1906/summary/?mobile-app=true&theme=wiki](https://www.nobelprize.org/prizes/medicine/1906/summary/?mobile-app=true&theme=wiki)

Q: What did microscopic staining help neuroscientists do?
A) Make every cell transparent  B) Distinguish cells and their fine structures*  C) Replace every microscope  D) Remove the need for evidence
Why: Staining makes otherwise difficult structures easier to see.

Q: What is the difference between antisepsis and asepsis?
A) Both mean giving pain relief  B) Asepsis means deliberately adding bacteria  C) Antisepsis reduces microbes; asepsis aims to prevent contamination*  D) Antisepsis means imaging bones
Why: Both reduce infection risk through different approaches.

Q: Why was microscope development important to medicine?
A) All diseases became instantly curable  B) Anatomy no longer mattered  C) Clinical observation became useless  D) Cells and microbes could be examined*
Why: Microscopy revealed structures and organisms beyond unaided vision.

Q: Why are historical human experiments judged critically today?
A) Consent and protection of participants*  B) Results excuse every harm  C) Children never need protection  D) Evidence removes all ethical duties
Why: Modern research requires attention to consent, risk and welfare.

Q: What distinguishes a discovery from a clinical treatment?
A) Every laboratory result is a proven cure  B) Safety, benefit and practical use still need testing*  C) Treatments never need evidence  D) All discoveries work in all patients
Why: Clinical usefulness requires evidence beyond an initial observation.

Q: Why can historical medical theories change?
A) It becomes old  B) Its author is unpopular  C) Better evidence conflicts with it*  D) A new name sounds better
Why: Explanations should fit the best available evidence.

Q: Which statement avoids an oversimplified history of medicine?
A) Every advance has one isolated inventor  B) Old knowledge was always worthless  C) Progress never involves disagreement  D) They often build on teamwork and earlier knowledge*
Why: Medical knowledge accumulates through many contributors and revisions.
